0.title: Ezra: The God Who Rebuilds
0.overview:
The book of Ezra opens in the middle of a sentence. In the Hebrew Bible, Chronicles stands last, and its final words are a Persian king's decree breaking off at Let him go up. Ezra repeats the decree almost word for word and finishes it: go up to Jerusalem, and rebuild the house of the LORD. The exile was not the end of the story. It was a sentence God had not yet completed.

Ezra and Nehemiah were one book in the Hebrew canon, later divided in Christian Bibles, and together they tell the story of the people who came home. Ezra is two stories a lifetime apart. Chapters 1-6 are the first return under Cyrus in 538 BC, led by Zerubbabel, the heir of David, and Jeshua, the high priest: the altar rebuilt among the ruins, the foundation laid to the sound of weeping and shouting, sixteen years of opposition and silence, the preaching of Haggai and Zechariah, and the second temple finished and dedicated in 516 or 515, some seventy years after Solomon's was burned. Then three words — Now after this (7:1) — carry the reader across fifty-eight years, the years of the book of Esther, to 458 BC, when Ezra the priest and scribe walks nine hundred miles from Babylon with the law of God in his hand.

Two things are invisible in an English Bible, and a reader should know them before starting. First, chapters 4-6 are not in strict date order: 4:6-23 gathers opposition from the later reigns of Xerxes and Artaxerxes, to show the reader a pattern rather than an incident. Second, from 4:8 to 6:18, and again at 7:12-26, the book is written in Aramaic, the language of the Persian letters it quotes.

The book is built on a few words used again and again. God stirred the spirit of Cyrus, and of the families who went home (1:1, 5), and later of the builders through Haggai's preaching. The hand of the LORD was on Ezra — six times in chapters 7 and 8, every time explaining something that should not have happened. And Ezra set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel (7:10): study, do, teach, in that order.

It ends on its hardest chapter. The returned community had married into households that served other gods — the issue was worship, never blood; Ruth the Moabite is David's great-grandmother — and chapter 10 records the painful covenant to put those marriages away. A Christian reader must read that chapter with the apostle's answer beside it: a believer married to an unbeliever should not divorce, for the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife ... as it is, they are holy (1 Cor 7:12-14).

Through it all runs the God who rebuilds. He keeps the names of the families who come home, turns the hearts of emperors, answers a prayer that asks for nothing, and brings his people back to the place where sin is dealt with. The house they built was smaller than Solomon's, and the old men wept to see it. It was the only one of the two that the Son of God ever walked into.

1.title: The Stirred Heart: Cyrus, the Decree, and the Upward Call
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom and also put it in writing:<sup>2</sup>"Thus says Cyrus king of Persia: The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah.<sup>3</sup>Whoever is among you of all his people, may his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and rebuild the house of the LORD, the God of Israel— he is the God who is in Jerusalem.<sup>4</sup>And let each survivor, in whatever place he sojourns, be assisted by the men of his place with silver and gold, with goods and with beasts, besides freewill offerings for the house of God that is in Jerusalem."<sup>5</sup>Then rose up the heads of the fathers' houses of Judah and Benjamin, and the priests and the Levites, everyone whose spirit God had stirred to go up to rebuild the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem.<sup>6</sup>And all who were about them aided them with vessels of silver, with gold, with goods, with beasts, and with costly wares, besides all that was freely offered.<sup>7</sup>Cyrus the king also brought out the vessels of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem and placed in the house of his gods.<sup>8</sup>Cyrus king of Persia brought these out in the charge of Mithredath the treasurer, who counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah.<sup>9</sup>And this was the number of them: 30 basins of gold, 1,000 basins of silver, 29 censers,<sup>10</sup>30 bowls of gold, 410 bowls of silver, and 1,000 other vessels;<sup>11</sup>all the vessels of gold and of silver were 5,400. All these did Sheshbazzar bring up, when the exiles were brought up from Babylonia to Jerusalem.
1.overview: Ezra opens by finishing the sentence 2 Chronicles broke off. In the first year of Cyrus, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirs the emperor's spirit and he proclaims that the God of heaven has charged him to build a house at Jerusalem: whoever belongs to that God, let him go up — and let those who stay help those who go (vv. 1-4). Then the same verb again: the family heads, priests and Levites rise up, everyone whose spirit God had stirred, and their neighbours load them with silver and gold as Egypt once did (vv. 5-6). Cyrus brings out the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had set in his own god's house, and they are counted out by a Persian treasurer to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah and carried home (vv. 7-11).
1.theology:
The chapter is built on one verb used twice. The LORD stirred up Cyrus (v. 1), and God stirred the spirits of the families who went (v. 5). Providence opened the road in the wide world; grace got particular people onto it. Neither the emperor's decree nor the exiles' decision is the first cause of the return. God is, and both Jeremiah's seventy years and Isaiah's naming of Cyrus arrive together to say so.

The return is written as a second exodus: a people leaving a foreign land with their neighbours' silver and gold (Exod 12:35-36), carrying the holy things, going up to the place of God's presence. And the vessels that had served as a pagan king's trophies are counted back to the last bowl — nothing given to God is finally lost to Babylon.
1.examples:
The last three words of 2 Chronicles are the middle of Ezra's third verse; the new book finishes the old book's sentence.

Cyrus's own clay cylinder credits Marduk. Scripture does not argue with it — it simply says who was moving him.

An emperor's permission opened the road, and it still took God stirring each family before anyone sold a house and started walking.

Those who stayed in Babylon were not condemned; they loaded the carts of the ones who went.

The cups Belshazzar drank from on the night Babylon fell were counted out by a Persian treasurer and carried back to Jerusalem.

The six items on the list add up to 2,499, and the total given is 5,400. Somebody counted, and the text keeps both figures.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The LORD Stirred Up the Spirit of Cyrus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus, and he proclaimed it in speech and in writing (v. 1): the God of heaven has given him the kingdoms of the earth and charged him to build a house at Jerusalem (v. 2). Whoever is among you of all his people, may his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem ... and rebuild the house of the LORD (v. 3). And those who stay are to help the ones who go, with silver and gold, goods and animals, and freewill offerings for the house (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The first three verses of Ezra are the last two verses of 2 Chronicles, almost word for word — and Chronicles breaks off at Let him go up. Ezra picks up the same sentence and finishes it: go up to Jerusalem, and rebuild the house. The book that closes the Hebrew Bible and the book that opens the return are stitched together in the middle of a single decree.
verseByVerse.examples: Isaiah had named this king before he was born: who says of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose (Isa 44:28). And Jeremiah had put a number on the exile — seventy years (Jer 25:11; 29:10). Verse 1 says both prophecies came due on the same day, in the mouth of a Persian who, as far as we know, had never read either.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom and also put it in writing: "Thus says Cyrus king of Persia: The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whoever is among you of all his people, may his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and rebuild the house of the LORD, the God of Israel— he is the God who is in Jerusalem. And let each survivor, in whatever place he sojourns, be assisted by the men of his place with silver and gold, with goods and with beasts, besides freewill offerings for the house of God that is in Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom and also put it in writing.

A reader coming straight from 2 Chronicles has read this sentence before. It is the last verse but one of that book, almost word for word, and the decree that follows is the last verse of it. Chronicles stops dead in the middle of Cyrus's proclamation, on three words: Let him go up. In the Hebrew Bible, where Chronicles stands last, those are the final words of the Old Testament.

Ezra takes the same sentence and finishes it. Let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and rebuild the house of the LORD, the God of Israel. The seam between the two books runs through the middle of a single royal decree, and the join is meant to be seen. The exile was not the end of the story. It was a sentence that had not yet been completed.

And the first thing verse 1 tells us is why it happened. Not because Persia had a policy on resettling conquered peoples, though it did. Not because Cyrus was generous, though he may have been. That the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled. Jeremiah had said seventy years (Jer 25:11; 29:10), and he had said it while Jerusalem was still standing and nobody believed him. Isaiah, earlier still, had given the rescuer a name: who says of Cyrus, He is my shepherd (Isa 44:28).

Cyrus himself left a clay cylinder, which still exists, crediting his conquest of Babylon to the god Marduk. The Bible does not argue with his inscription. It simply tells us who was actually moving him: the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus. A man can be the instrument of a God he has never met, and his own account of his motives is not the last word.

The decree has two halves. Whoever wants to go, let him go. And whoever stays, let him help: let each survivor, in whatever place he sojourns, be assisted by the men of his place with silver and gold, with goods and with beasts. Survivors — that is the word for the exiles now, the ones who came through. The emperor has written the return and its funding into the same order.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — Everyone Whose Spirit God Had Stirred
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then rose up the heads of the fathers' houses of Judah and Benjamin, and the priests and the Levites, everyone whose spirit God had stirred to go up (v. 5). Their neighbours load them with silver, gold, goods, animals and costly things, besides freewill offerings (v. 6). Cyrus brings out the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had carried off and set in the house of his gods (v. 7), and his treasurer Mithredath counts them out to Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah (v. 8): basins, censers and bowls of gold and silver (vv. 9-10), all the vessels of gold and of silver were 5,400, carried up when the exiles came home (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The same verb runs through verses 1 and 5. God stirred the spirit of the most powerful man on earth, and God stirred the spirits of ordinary families in Babylon. The emperor's stirring produced a permission; theirs produced a journey. A decree can open a road, and only God can make anybody want to walk down it.
verseByVerse.examples: Add up verses 9 and 10: thirty basins, a thousand, twenty-nine censers, thirty bowls, four hundred and ten, a thousand others. That is 2,499. Verse 11 says the whole came to 5,400. The list names the principal pieces; the total counts everything, and the text does not explain the difference.

verseByVerse.quote: Then rose up the heads of the fathers' houses of Judah and Benjamin, and the priests and the Levites, everyone whose spirit God had stirred to go up to rebuild the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem. And all who were about them aided them with vessels of silver, with gold, with goods, with beasts, and with costly wares, besides all that was freely offered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then rose up the heads of the fathers' houses of Judah and Benjamin, and the priests and the Levites, everyone whose spirit God had stirred to go up to rebuild the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem.

Everyone whose spirit God had stirred. It is the verb of verse 1, used again four verses later, and the repetition is the whole theology of the chapter.

God stirred the spirit of an emperor, and the emperor produced a permission. But a permission moves nobody. Families who had been born in Babylon, who had houses there and vineyards and trades and grandparents buried there, had to decide to sell up and walk nine hundred miles to a city most of them had never seen, which was a ruin. What got them onto the road was the same hand that got Cyrus to pick up his pen.

That is the pattern of every return to God, then and since. Doors are opened by providence in the wide world — a decree, a circumstance, a chance. But nobody goes through a door because it is open. They go because something has been stirred in them, and the Bible never lets us take the credit for that part.

Not everyone went. Most of the Jews in Babylon stayed, and the text does not condemn them. Jeremiah himself had told the exiles to build houses, plant gardens and seek the welfare of the city (Jer 29:5-7), and many had done precisely that. What the text does record is what the stayers did for the goers: all who were about them aided them with vessels of silver, with gold, with goods, with beasts, and with costly wares, besides all that was freely offered.

Anyone who has ever supported someone else's calling will recognise the arrangement. Some are stirred to go, and some are stirred to load the cart. And any reader of Exodus will recognise the silver and gold: Israel left Egypt carrying the valuables of its neighbours too (Exod 12:35-36). A second exodus has begun, and it starts the way the first one did.

verseByVerse.quote: Cyrus the king also brought out the vessels of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem and placed in the house of his gods. Cyrus king of Persia brought these out in the charge of Mithredath the treasurer, who counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah. And this was the number of them: 30 basins of gold, 1,000 basins of silver, 29 censers, 30 bowls of gold, 410 bowls of silver, and 1,000 other vessels; all the vessels of gold and of silver were 5,400. All these did Sheshbazzar bring up, when the exiles were brought up from Babylonia to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cyrus the king also brought out the vessels of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem and placed in the house of his gods.

The vessels. Anyone who has just finished 2 Chronicles watched them go: part of the vessels with Jehoiakim, the precious vessels with Jehoiachin, and at the fall of the city all the vessels of the house of God, great and small (2 Chr 36:7, 10, 18). Nebuchadnezzar set them up in his own temple as trophies — the kitchenware of a god he had beaten. And on the last night of Babylon, Belshazzar called for them at his feast, and he and his lords and his women drank wine from them and praised gods of gold and silver, while a hand wrote on the wall (Dan 5:2-5).

Now they come out again, and they come out counted. Cyrus king of Persia brought these out in the charge of Mithredath the treasurer, who counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah. A named official on one side, a named recipient on the other, and a list between them. It is the same care with holy things that sent two men to empty Joash's chest together (2 Chr 24:11).

Then the inventory, and a careful reader should do the sum. Thirty basins of gold, a thousand of silver, twenty-nine censers, thirty gold bowls, four hundred and ten silver bowls, a thousand other vessels. That comes to 2,499. And verse 11 says all the vessels of gold and of silver were 5,400.

The text does not explain the gap, and it is more honest to say so than to pretend the figures agree. The likeliest reading is that the list names the principal pieces and the total counts everything that went back, including the smaller items nobody troubled to itemise. It is also true that numbers are the most fragile thing in any ancient manuscript; a single stroke changes a figure, and scribes copied these by hand for centuries. Nothing in the chapter turns on the discrepancy. What turns on the verse is that somebody counted.

Who was Sheshbazzar? He hands over the vessels here and then all but vanishes. Chapter 5 says he laid the foundations of the house (5:16); chapter 3 says Zerubbabel did (3:8-10). Some take them for one man with a Babylonian name and a Hebrew one; others for two leaders in succession. The text leaves it open, and so should we.

What it does not leave open is the point of the list. Every cup Belshazzar drank from was counted out, carried nine hundred miles, and delivered. Not one piece of what belonged to the house of God was written off as lost to Babylon. And that is how the Lord Jesus speaks of the people his Father has given him: this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day (John 6:39). The vessels were counted out of Babylon to the last bowl. He counts his people the same way, and none of them is left behind in the house of another god.

2.overview: The roll of those who came home: eleven named leaders headed by Zerubbabel and Jeshua (vv. 1-2), the lay families by clan (vv. 3-20) and by town — Bethlehem, Anathoth, Bethel and Ai, Jericho (vv. 21-35) — then 4,289 priests (vv. 36-39) against only 74 Levites, with 128 singers and 139 gatekeepers (vv. 40-42), and 392 temple servants and sons of Solomon's servants (vv. 43-58). Six hundred and fifty-two people who could not prove they were Israelites came anyway, and three priestly families who could not find their names in the register were barred from the priesthood until a priest could consult Urim and Thummim (vv. 59-63). The whole assembly is given as 42,360, with servants, singers and eight thousand animals (vv. 64-67), and on arrival the heads of families gave according to their ability to rebuild the house on its site (vv. 68-70).
2.theology:
The list is the answer to the exile's question. Babylon was meant to dissolve Israel into an empire, and seventy years later these families could still name their ancestors and their villages. God had not preserved an idea of Israel; he had preserved the sons of Parosh and the men of Anathoth — the town where Jeremiah bought a field during the siege as a pledge that fields would be bought there again (Jer 32:15).

Verses 59-63 hold law and mercy together. The unprovable are counted among the people; the unprovable priests are barred from the altar until God gives a word. The standard is not relaxed and nobody is thrown out. And the whole arrangement waits for a Priest whose office rests not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life (Heb 7:16).
2.examples:
Verse 2 names eleven leaders; Nehemiah's copy of the list has twelve.

The families added together come to 29,818; the stated total is 42,360, and the text keeps both figures.

A hundred and twenty-eight men of Anathoth came home to the town where Jeremiah had bought a field while Babylon was at the gates.

There were seventy-four Levites for 4,289 priests; the men with the hardest work mostly stayed behind.

A family called the sons of Sisera came home to serve at the altar.

A priest took the name of his famous father-in-law, and three generations later his descendants could not find themselves in the register.

The first thing the families did on reaching the ruins was give money toward a building that was not there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–35 — The Men of the People of Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now these were the people of the province who came up out of the captivity, each to his own town (v. 1), led by eleven named men, Zerubbabel and Jeshua first (v. 2). Then the lay families, counted twice over: by the name of a clan ancestor — the sons of Parosh, 2,172; of Pahath-moab, 2,812; of Bigvai, 2,056 (vv. 3-20) — and then by the town their families came from: the sons of Bethlehem, 123. The men of Netophah, 56. The men of Anathoth, 128, Bethel and Ai, Jericho, and last and largest Senaah, 3,630 (vv. 21-35).
verseByVerse.theology: The list is not an interruption of the story; it is the evidence the story needed. Babylon had been supposed to dissolve these families into an empire, and seventy years later they could still tell you who their great-grandfather was and which village he farmed. God had not kept an idea of Israel through the exile. He had kept the sons of Parosh.
verseByVerse.examples: Anathoth is on the list — 128 men of it. That is Jeremiah's town, and while Babylon was besieging Jerusalem he bought a field there, paid in silver before witnesses, as God's pledge that fields would be bought and sold in this land again (Jer 32:15). Here are the buyers.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these were the people of the province who came up out of the captivity of those exiles whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried captive to Babylonia. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town. They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah. The number of the men of the people of Israel:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now these were the people of the province who came up out of the captivity of those exiles whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried captive to Babylonia. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town.

Each to his own town. Seventy years after the deportations, these families still knew which town was theirs. Most of the people walking back had never seen it; they were going home to a place they knew only as a name their grandparents used.

Modern readers skim a list like this, so it helps to know why the Bible keeps them. Every name was the answer to a question the exile had asked: whether Israel would survive as a people or melt into Babylon the way every other conquered nation had. This chapter is the answer, family by family.

Eleven leaders are named in verse 2, Zerubbabel and Jeshua at the head — the heir of David and the high priest, the two offices the community will be rebuilt around. Nehemiah's copy of the same list has twelve names (Neh 7:7), and twelve is plainly the point: a returning Israel led by one man for each tribe. Somewhere in the copying of Ezra's list, one name has dropped out.

And the Nehemiah and Mordecai on the list are not the famous ones. The Nehemiah who rebuilt the walls and the Mordecai of the book of Esther lived two and three generations later. These are other men who happened to share the name, and the text does not trouble to distinguish them because its first readers knew exactly who they were.

verseByVerse.quote: the sons of Parosh, 2,172. The sons of Shephatiah, 372. The sons of Arah, 775. The sons of Pahath-moab, namely the sons of Jeshua and Joab, 2,812. The sons of Elam, 1,254. The sons of Zattu, 945. The sons of Zaccai, 760. The sons of Bani, 642. The sons of Bebai, 623. The sons of Azgad, 1,222. The sons of Adonikam, 666. The sons of Bigvai, 2,056. The sons of Adin, 454. The sons of Ater, namely of Hezekiah, 98. The sons of Bezai, 323. The sons of Jorah, 112. The sons of Hashum, 223. The sons of Gibbar, 95.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the families, each under the name of an ancestor and each with a figure beside it. The sons of Parosh, 2,172. The sons of Pahath-moab, 2,812. The sons of Elam, 1,254. The sons of Bigvai, 2,056. Down to the sons of Gibbar, 95.

Eighteen family groups, 15,604 men between them, and the variation is the story. Some families came home two thousand strong. Some came home with fewer than a hundred — the sons of Ater, of Hezekiah's line, ninety-eight. Behind each figure is a set of decisions made in Babylon: who went and who stayed, which cousins sold up and which did not.

Somebody kept these records through seventy years in a foreign country, and somebody else kept them after that. That in itself is a kind of faith. A family that goes on writing down its descent in exile is a family that expects to go home.

And the God of the Bible is interested in exactly this level of detail. He did not rescue the Jewish people in the abstract. He rescued the sons of Zattu, nine hundred and forty-five of them, and had it written down.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Bethlehem, 123. The men of Netophah, 56. The men of Anathoth, 128. The sons of Azmaveth, 42. The sons of Kiriath-arim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, 743. The sons of Ramah and Geba, 621. The men of Michmas, 122. The men of Bethel and Ai, 223. The sons of Nebo, 52. The sons of Magbish, 156. The sons of the other Elam, 1,254. The sons of Harim, 320. The sons of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, 725. The sons of Jericho, 345. The sons of Senaah, 3,630.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the counting changes, from the name of a family to the name of a town. The sons of Bethlehem, 123. The men of Netophah, 56. The men of Anathoth, 128. Fifteen place-names, 8,540 men.

Bethlehem, a hundred and twenty-three of them, going back to David's town, where Micah had said a ruler would one day come from.

Anathoth is the one to stop at. It was Jeremiah's town — he was of the priests who were in Anathoth (Jer 1:1) — and during the last siege, with the Babylonian army at the walls and the country about to be lost, God told him to buy a field there. He weighed out the silver, signed the deed before witnesses, sealed it in a jar, and said why: houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land (Jer 32:15). Everyone watching thought he was mad.

Here are a hundred and twenty-eight men of Anathoth walking home to farm it.

Bethel and Ai are on the list too, two hundred and twenty-three men — Bethel where Jeroboam set up his golden calf, Ai where Israel lost its first battle in Canaan because of one man's hidden theft. Places with long and mixed histories, and the people coming home to them are not asked to account for any of it. Jericho sends three hundred and forty-five. And the largest single group of all is the last: Senaah, 3,630, a town that is otherwise almost unknown.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–63 — Priests, Levites, and Those Who Could Not Prove It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four priestly families, 4,289 in all (vv. 36-39). Then seventy-four Levites (v. 40), 128 singers of the sons of Asaph (v. 41) and 139 gatekeepers (v. 42). The temple servants and the sons of Solomon's servants, listed family by family, come to 392 (vv. 43-58). Then 652 people from the towns of the east who could not prove their fathers' houses or their descent, whether they belonged to Israel (vv. 59-60), and three priestly families who could not find themselves in the register (vv. 61-62) — excluded from the priesthood as unclean until a priest to consult Urim and Thummim should arise (v. 63).
verseByVerse.theology: The priests who could not prove their descent were not expelled from the people. They were barred from the priesthood and from the most holy food, and told to wait for a word from God. Hebrews names the priest they were waiting for without knowing it: one who holds the office not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life (Heb 7:16).
verseByVerse.examples: Seventy-four Levites came home against 4,289 priests — about one to every fifty-eight. The men whose work was the heavy, unglamorous service of the house mostly stayed in Babylon, and when Ezra gathers his own caravan eighty years later he will look for Levites and find none (8:15).

verseByVerse.quote: The priests: the sons of Jedaiah, of the house of Jeshua, 973. The sons of Immer, 1,052. The sons of Pashhur, 1,247. The sons of Harim, 1,017.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests: the sons of Jedaiah, of the house of Jeshua, 973. The sons of Immer, 1,052. The sons of Pashhur, 1,247. The sons of Harim, 1,017.

Four priestly families, 4,289 men. That is roughly one in seven of every man on the list — a huge proportion, and it tells you what kind of return this was. It was a return organised around a building that did not yet exist. The families whose whole life was the altar came home in numbers, because without the altar the rest of it made no sense.

The first of them is of the house of Jeshua — the high priest named in verse 2. The line of Aaron has come through the exile unbroken, and its head is standing at the front of the column beside the heir of David.

verseByVerse.quote: The Levites: the sons of Jeshua and Kadmiel, of the sons of Hodaviah, 74. The singers: the sons of Asaph, 128. The sons of the gatekeepers: the sons of Shallum, the sons of Ater, the sons of Talmon, the sons of Akkub, the sons of Hatita, and the sons of Shobai, in all 139.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a figure that tells a different story. The Levites: the sons of Jeshua and Kadmiel, of the sons of Hodaviah, 74.

Seventy-four. Against 4,289 priests. About one Levite for every fifty-eight priests, when the whole temple system assumed the Levites would far outnumber them — they were the ones who did the heavy work of the house, the carrying, the cleaning, the slaughtering, the teaching.

The men whose service was hardest and least honoured mostly stayed in Babylon. It is not hard to see why: a Levite had no inheritance of land to go back to, only a job in a ruin. And the shortage did not go away. When Ezra assembles his own caravan in chapter 8, he reviews the people at the river and finds none of the sons of Levi there at all (8:15), and has to send a delegation to fetch some.

Add the singers and the gatekeepers, and the whole house of Levi on the list is 341 men. The singers are the sons of Asaph, a hundred and twenty-eight of them — the guild David set apart for the music of the house, still singing, still counted, after two generations in a country where their harps hung on the willows.

verseByVerse.quote: The temple servants: the sons of Ziha, the sons of Hasupha, the sons of Tabbaoth, the sons of Keros, the sons of Siaha, the sons of Padon, the sons of Lebanah, the sons of Hagabah, the sons of Akkub, the sons of Hagab, the sons of Shamlai, the sons of Hanan, the sons of Giddel, the sons of Gahar, the sons of Reaiah, the sons of Rezin, the sons of Nekoda, the sons of Gazzam, the sons of Uzza, the sons of Paseah, the sons of Besai, the sons of Asnah, the sons of Meunim, the sons of Nephisim, the sons of Bakbuk, the sons of Hakupha, the sons of Harhur, the sons of Bazluth, the sons of Mehida, the sons of Harsha, the sons of Barkos, the sons of Sisera, the sons of Temah, the sons of Neziah, and the sons of Hatipha. The sons of Solomon's servants: the sons of Sotai, the sons of Hassophereth, the sons of Peruda, the sons of Jaalah, the sons of Darkon, the sons of Giddel, the sons of Shephatiah, the sons of Hattil, the sons of Pochereth-hazzebaim, and the sons of Ami. All the temple servants and the sons of Solomon's servants were 392.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the longest run of names in the chapter, and the most easily skipped: the temple servants, family after family, and the sons of Solomon's servants.

We know less about these people than about anyone else on the list. The temple servants are often connected with the Gibeonites, whom Joshua made cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD (Josh 9:27), and Solomon's servants with the non-Israelite peoples he conscripted as labour (2 Chr 8:7-9). If that is right, a good many of these families were not Israelite by descent at all. They had been attached to the house of God for centuries, and when the house was destroyed they went into exile with it, and now they are coming back to it.

One name in the middle of the list stops a reader: the sons of Sisera. It is the name of Jabin's general, the man Jael killed with a tent peg. Nothing in the text says this family descended from him. But a family carrying the name of Israel's old enemy is walking home from Babylon to serve at the altar of Israel's God, and the list gives them a line of their own.

All of them together come to 392 — a figure that includes families whose only claim on the house of God was that they had served in it. The book does not rank them below the priests. They are counted.

verseByVerse.quote: The following were those who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer, though they could not prove their fathers' houses or their descent, whether they belonged to Israel: the sons of Delaiah, the sons of Tobiah, and the sons of Nekoda, 652. Also, of the sons of the priests: the sons of Habaiah, the sons of Hakkoz, and the sons of Barzillai (who had taken a wife from the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called by their name). These sought their registration among those enrolled in the genealogies, but they were not found there, and so they were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. The governor told them that they were not to partake of the most holy food, until there should be a priest to consult Urim and Thummim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now five verses that are hard and tender at once.

The following were those who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer, though they could not prove their fathers' houses or their descent, whether they belonged to Israel. Six hundred and fifty-two people who had lost their paperwork in the catastrophe, who could not say for certain that they were Israelites at all — and they came anyway. They are on the list. Nobody turned them back at the border.

Then three priestly families, and one of them has a story. The sons of Barzillai (who had taken a wife from the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called by their name). Barzillai the Gileadite was the old man who fed David and his men at Mahanaim when David was fleeing from Absalom, and whom David wanted to bring to Jerusalem and honour (2 Sam 19:31-39). Generations later a priest married into that famous family and took its name — and his descendants could no longer be found in the priestly register under their own.

These sought their registration among those enrolled in the genealogies, but they were not found there, and so they were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. Seeking their name and not finding it. It is one of the saddest sentences in the book.

And yet notice exactly what was done. They were not expelled from the people. The governor barred them from the priesthood and from the most holy food, and told them to wait: until there should be a priest to consult Urim and Thummim. Nobody in authority was willing to decide by sentiment. They waited for a word from God.

And for at least one of those families the waiting ended. Eighty years later, when Ezra's caravan reached Jerusalem, the temple treasure was weighed into the hands of Meremoth the priest, son of Uriah (8:33) — and Nehemiah gives his full line: son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz (Neh 3:4). The sons of Hakkoz, who could not find their names in 538, were serving as priests by 458. The text never tells us how.

They were waiting, though they could not know it, for a Priest of a different kind altogether. The letter to the Hebrews says of Jesus that he came from Judah, a tribe Moses never connected with the priesthood at all, and that he is a priest not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life (Heb 7:16). The register that shut out the sons of Barzillai could not have admitted him either. His priesthood does not rest on a document that can be lost in a fire, and neither does the standing of anyone who comes to God through him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole assembly together was 42,360, besides 7,337 servants and 200 singers (vv. 64-65), with 736 horses, 245 mules, 435 camels and 6,720 donkeys (vv. 66-67). When they reached the ruined house, some of the heads of families made freewill offerings for the house of God, to erect it on its site; according to their ability they gave 61,000 darics of gold, 5,000 minas of silver and a hundred priests' garments (vv. 68-69). Then everyone went home to his own town (v. 70).
verseByVerse.theology: They gave according to their ability — not a flat levy, not an equal share, but proportion. It is the same measure Paul uses of the Macedonians, who gave according to their means and beyond them (2 Cor 8:3). And they gave to rebuild the house on its site, on the same rock where Solomon's had stood.
verseByVerse.examples: Add up the list and it comes to 29,818. Verse 64 says 42,360. The heading says it is counting the men of the people of Israel, so the likeliest reading is that the total takes in people the family lists never itemised. The text does not explain the gap, and it leaves both figures standing.

verseByVerse.quote: The whole assembly together was 42,360, besides their male and female servants, of whom there were 7,337, and they had 200 male and female singers. Their horses were 736, their mules were 245, their camels were 435, and their donkeys were 6,720.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole assembly together was 42,360.

Do the sum and it does not come out. Every figure in the list, families, towns, priests, Levites, servants and the unprovable six hundred and fifty-two, adds up to 29,818. The stated total is 12,542 higher. The chapter's heading says it is counting the men of the people of Israel, so the likeliest reading is that the grand total takes in people the clan lists never itemised. Nehemiah's copy has the same grand total and different figures in the detail. The text does not explain the difference, and it is better to say so than to force the arithmetic.

Then the rest of the caravan. Besides their male and female servants, of whom there were 7,337, and they had 200 male and female singers. And the animals, counted as carefully as the people: 736 horses, 245 mules, 435 camels and 6,720 donkeys — more than eight thousand beasts, most of them donkeys, which is what a column of families carrying everything they own over nine hundred miles actually looks like.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the heads of families, when they came to the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem, made freewill offerings for the house of God, to erect it on its site. According to their ability they gave to the treasury of the work 61,000 darics of gold, 5,000 minas of silver, and 100 priests' garments. Now the priests, the Levites, some of the people, the singers, the gatekeepers, and the temple servants lived in their towns, and all the rest of Israel in their towns.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the heads of families, when they came to the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem, made freewill offerings for the house of God, to erect it on its site.

When they came to the house of the LORD — which was a heap of burned stone. The first thing these families did on reaching Jerusalem, before they had roofs over their own heads, was give money toward a building that was not there.

To erect it on its site. Not somewhere more convenient, not a fresh start on cleaner ground. On the same rock where Solomon's house had stood, where David had bought a threshing floor and Abraham had once taken his son. The return was not a new religion. It was the old one, rebuilt on its own foundations.

According to their ability they gave to the treasury of the work 61,000 darics of gold, 5,000 minas of silver, and 100 priests' garments. According to their ability. Not an equal levy, not a flat figure per household. Each gave in proportion to what he had, which is exactly how Paul describes the Macedonian churches, who gave according to their means ... and beyond their means (2 Cor 8:3).

And the chapter ends quietly. All the rest of Israel in their towns. Seventy verses of names, and the last one sends everybody home to start ploughing.

A roll of names like this one is the Old Testament's picture of something the Lord Jesus told his disciples to care about more than any success they could see. When they came back exhilarated from their first mission, he told them not to rejoice in what they had achieved, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). Babylon could not blot out the sons of Parosh. Nothing can blot out a name he has written down.

3.title: The Altar Before the Temple: Worship, Weeping, and the Shout of Joy
3.text: <sup>1</sup>When the seventh month came, and the children of Israel were in the towns, the people gathered as one man to Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>Then arose Jeshua the son of Jozadak, with his fellow priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel with his kinsmen, and they built the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings on it, as it is written in the Law of Moses the man of God.<sup>3</sup>They set the altar in its place, for fear was on them because of the peoples of the lands, and they offered burnt offerings on it to the LORD, burnt offerings morning and evening.<sup>4</sup>And they kept the Feast of Booths, as it is written, and offered the daily burnt offerings by number according to the rule, as each day required,<sup>5</sup>and after that the regular burnt offerings, the offerings at the new moon and at all the appointed feasts of the LORD, and the offerings of everyone who made a freewill offering to the LORD.<sup>6</sup>From the first day of the seventh month they began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD. But the foundation of the temple of the LORD was not yet laid.<sup>7</sup>So they gave money to the masons and the carpenters, and food, drink, and oil to the Sidonians and the Tyrians to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea, to Joppa, according to the grant that they had from Cyrus king of Persia.<sup>8</sup>Now in the second year after their coming to the house of God at Jerusalem, in the second month, Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak made a beginning, together with the rest of their kinsmen, the priests and the Levites and all who had come to Jerusalem from the captivity. They appointed the Levites, from twenty years old and upward, to supervise the work of the house of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>And Jeshua with his sons and his brothers, and Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, together supervised the workmen in the house of God, along with the sons of Henadad and the Levites, their sons and brothers.<sup>10</sup>And when the builders laid the foundation of the temple of the LORD, the priests in their vestments came forward with trumpets, and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise the LORD, according to the directions of David king of Israel.<sup>11</sup>And they sang responsively, praising and giving thanks to the LORD, "For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel." And all the people shouted with a great shout when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid.<sup>12</sup>But many of the priests and Levites and heads of fathers' houses, old men who had seen the first house, wept with a loud voice when they saw the foundation of this house being laid, though many shouted aloud for joy,<sup>13</sup>so that the people could not distinguish the sound of the joyful shout from the sound of the people's weeping, for the people shouted with a great shout, and the sound was heard far away.
3.overview: In the seventh month the returned families gather as one man, and the first thing they build is not a house or a wall but the altar, set in its place for fear was on them, with the morning and evening offerings restored (vv. 1-3). They keep Booths bull by bull as the law requires, restart the whole sacrificial calendar — but the foundation of the temple of the LORD was not yet laid — and order cedar from Tyre and Sidon by sea to Joppa, exactly as Solomon did (vv. 4-7). In the second month of the second year the foundation is laid under Levites appointed by David's rule, the priests blow trumpets and the sons of Asaph sing the old refrain, For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel (vv. 8-11). The old men who had seen Solomon's house weep aloud, the young shout for joy, and the two sounds cannot be told apart — and the noise is heard far away (vv. 12-13).
3.theology:
The altar comes before the house. For twenty years the returned community worshipped at an altar standing among ruins, and the order is the gospel's: the place where sin is dealt with comes first, and the dwelling of God is built around it. And verse 3 makes fear the reason for worship, not the obstacle to it.

Verse 11 is the refrain sung when the cloud filled Solomon's house (2 Chr 5:13) and when the fire fell (7:3), now sung over bare foundation stones with neither. God's steadfast love was never true because the glory was visible.

Verses 12-13 hold grief and joy in one sound, and neither is rebuked. Haggai later granted the old men's grief in full (Hag 2:3) and answered it with a promise: the latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former (Hag 2:9). The smaller house was the one the Son of God stood in.
3.examples:
The first thing the returnees built in Jerusalem was an altar in the open air on a hill of rubble.

They built it because they were afraid, and the text says so.

The Booths offering runs thirteen bulls, twelve, eleven — a countdown to seven — and the exiles kept it to the bull.

The cedar came from Lebanon by sea to Joppa, paid for in food, exactly as in Solomon's day.

Levites from twenty years old is David's rule, laid down in his last words (1 Chr 23:27).

Anyone old enough to remember the first temple standing was past sixty, and could see from the trench how much smaller the second would be.

The shouting and the weeping made one noise, and the noise brought the adversaries.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — They Set the Altar in Its Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the seventh month the people gather in Jerusalem as one man (v. 1). Jeshua the priest and Zerubbabel build the altar as it is written in the Law of Moses (v. 2), and they set the altar in its place, for fear was on them because of the peoples of the lands, and the morning and evening offerings begin again (v. 3). They keep Booths with its offerings by number according to the rule, as each day required, then the regular offerings and the freewill gifts (vv. 4-5) — But the foundation of the temple of the LORD was not yet laid (v. 6). They pay masons and carpenters, and send food, drink and oil to Tyre and Sidon for cedar floated to Joppa under Cyrus's grant (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The altar comes before the house. Before there are walls or a roof, before anyone knows whether the neighbours will let them build at all, the people restore the place where sin is dealt with and the day begins and ends with an offering. Access to God is not the reward for finishing the building. It is the first thing, and everything else is built around it.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 3 gives fear as the reason for the altar, not an obstacle to it: they set it up for fear was on them. A frightened people did not wait until they felt safe to worship. They worshipped because they did not.

verseByVerse.quote: When the seventh month came, and the children of Israel were in the towns, the people gathered as one man to Jerusalem. Then arose Jeshua the son of Jozadak, with his fellow priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel with his kinsmen, and they built the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings on it, as it is written in the Law of Moses the man of God. They set the altar in its place, for fear was on them because of the peoples of the lands, and they offered burnt offerings on it to the LORD, burnt offerings morning and evening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the seventh month came, and the children of Israel were in the towns, the people gathered as one man to Jerusalem.

The seventh month is the holy month of Israel's year: the trumpets on its first day, the Day of Atonement on its tenth, the Feast of Booths from its fifteenth (Lev 23). The families of the last chapter have barely unpacked — they are in the towns, scattered to the villages their grandparents came from — and when the month comes round they walk back up to Jerusalem together.

What they build first tells you everything.

Then arose Jeshua the son of Jozadak, with his fellow priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel with his kinsmen, and they built the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings on it, as it is written in the Law of Moses the man of God.

Not houses. Not walls. Not the temple — there is no temple, and there will not be one for twenty years. An altar, on the ruins, in the open air. And notice the order of the names: in the list of chapter 2 Zerubbabel came first, but when the work is an altar the high priest leads. They build it as it is written. After seventy years without a sacrifice, nobody improvises.

They set the altar in its place, for fear was on them because of the peoples of the lands, and they offered burnt offerings on it to the LORD, burnt offerings morning and evening.

For fear was on them. Read the grammar carefully, because it is the opposite of what one would expect. The fear is not described as an obstacle they overcame. It is given as the reason. They were a few thousand families in a ruined city surrounded by peoples who did not want them there, and so they built the altar.

This is what faith does with fear. It does not wait to feel safe before it worships; it worships because it does not feel safe, and it goes to the one place where the frightened are met by God. Whoever is afraid tonight has the same instruction these people had. Do not first fix the fear. Go to the altar.

And the offering goes up morning and evening. The daily sacrifice — the one that stopped when Ahaz shut the doors (2 Chr 29:7), and stopped again when the Babylonians burned the house — starts again. For the first time in two generations there is smoke over Jerusalem at dawn and at dusk that is not the smoke of a burning city.

verseByVerse.quote: And they kept the Feast of Booths, as it is written, and offered the daily burnt offerings by number according to the rule, as each day required, and after that the regular burnt offerings, the offerings at the new moon and at all the appointed feasts of the LORD, and the offerings of everyone who made a freewill offering to the LORD. From the first day of the seventh month they began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD. But the foundation of the temple of the LORD was not yet laid. So they gave money to the masons and the carpenters, and food, drink, and oil to the Sidonians and the Tyrians to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea, to Joppa, according to the grant that they had from Cyrus king of Persia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they kept the Feast of Booths, as it is written, and offered the daily burnt offerings by number according to the rule, as each day required.

Booths was the feast when Israel lived for a week in shelters made of branches to remember the wilderness. For these people it hardly needed acting out; most of them were still living in something temporary.

By number according to the rule. The law for that feast is precise to the point of strangeness. On the first day, thirteen bulls. On the second, twelve. One fewer every day, down to seven on the seventh: seventy bulls across the week (Num 29:13-32). The offering is a countdown, and the returned exiles kept it bull by bull. People who have just come back from losing everything to their own unfaithfulness do not treat the details as optional.

Then the regular offerings, the new moons, the appointed feasts, and the offerings of everyone who made a freewill offering to the LORD. The whole calendar restarted, and people gave more than the calendar asked.

From the first day of the seventh month they began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD. But the foundation of the temple of the LORD was not yet laid.

Hold that picture. An altar standing by itself on a hill of rubble, smoke rising from it twice a day, and all around it the burned stones of the house that used to be there. No walls, no roof, no Holy Place, no ark. Worship had come back before the building did, and the writer wants us to notice which came first.

Then they start on the building, and the way they go about it is a deliberate echo. So they gave money to the masons and the carpenters, and food, drink, and oil to the Sidonians and the Tyrians to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea, to Joppa.

That is Solomon's contract, almost clause for clause. Solomon paid Hiram of Tyre in wheat, barley, wine and oil, and Hiram cut cedar in Lebanon and brought it in rafts by sea to Joppa (2 Chr 2:10, 16). The same forest, the same Phoenician crews, the same payment in food, the same port. The second house is begun exactly the way the first one was.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The Sound Was Heard Far Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the second month of the second year Zerubbabel and Jeshua begin, with the Levites from twenty years old supervising the work (vv. 8-9). When the foundation is laid, the priests stand in their vestments with trumpets and the sons of Asaph with cymbals, according to the directions of David (v. 10), and they sing: For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel, and the people shout with a great shout (v. 11). But many of the priests and Levites and heads of fathers' houses, old men who had seen the first house, wept with a loud voice, while many shouted for joy (v. 12), so that the people could not distinguish the sound of the joyful shout from the sound of the people's weeping — and it was heard far away (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The song in verse 11 is the one Israel sang when the cloud filled Solomon's house so that the priests could not stand to minister (2 Chr 5:13), and again when the fire came down (7:3). Here there is no cloud and no fire — only a row of foundation stones in a ruined city — and they sing exactly the same words. His steadfast love endures forever did not depend on the glory being visible.
verseByVerse.examples: Both sounds were right. The old men were not faithless for weeping; they knew what had been lost and could see from the size of the foundation how much smaller this house would be. The young were not shallow for shouting; they had been born in exile, and any foundation at all was a miracle. God's people have always lived with both sounds at once, and this is the verse that gives them permission.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the second year after their coming to the house of God at Jerusalem, in the second month, Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak made a beginning, together with the rest of their kinsmen, the priests and the Levites and all who had come to Jerusalem from the captivity. They appointed the Levites, from twenty years old and upward, to supervise the work of the house of the LORD. And Jeshua with his sons and his brothers, and Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, together supervised the workmen in the house of God, along with the sons of Henadad and the Levites, their sons and brothers. And when the builders laid the foundation of the temple of the LORD, the priests in their vestments came forward with trumpets, and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise the LORD, according to the directions of David king of Israel. And they sang responsively, praising and giving thanks to the LORD, "For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel." And all the people shouted with a great shout when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in the second year after their coming to the house of God at Jerusalem, in the second month, Zerubbabel ... and Jeshua ... made a beginning.

The second month. Solomon, too, began to build in the second month (2 Chr 3:2). The writer keeps setting the new house down on the pattern of the old one.

They appointed the Levites, from twenty years old and upward, to supervise the work of the house of the LORD. That age is not an emergency concession. Moses set the Levites' service from twenty-five (Num 8:24), and David, at the end of his life, moved it to twenty: by the last words of David the sons of Levi were numbered from twenty years old and upward (1 Chr 23:27). The returnees are following David's order to the year. With seventy-four Levites in the whole caravan, they needed every one of them.

Then the foundation is laid, and the ceremony is carefully described. The priests in their vestments came forward with trumpets, and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise the LORD, according to the directions of David king of Israel. The sons of Asaph — the hundred and twenty-eight singers of 2:41 — are playing the instruments their great-great-grandfathers played, in the order David laid down.

And they sang responsively, praising and giving thanks to the LORD, For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel.

A reader who has come through Chronicles knows that song. The Levites sang it when the ark came to Jerusalem. They sang it at the dedication of Solomon's house, and at the moment they sang it the house was filled with a cloud, so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of God (2 Chr 5:13-14). The people sang it again on their faces when fire fell from heaven on the altar (7:3). Jehoshaphat's choir sang it marching out in front of his army (20:21).

Now it is sung over a row of foundation stones. There is no cloud. There is no fire. There is no ark, and there never will be again. And they sing exactly the same words, and add two of their own: toward Israel. His steadfast love endures forever, toward us — toward the people who were sent into exile for their sins and have just walked home.

That is what it means to believe the refrain. It was never true because the glory was visible. It was true in Babylon, where there was no altar at all, and it is true on a building site, and it is true on the worst morning of anyone's life. And all the people shouted with a great shout — the phrase used of Jericho, the day the walls came down (Josh 6:5).

verseByVerse.quote: But many of the priests and Levites and heads of fathers' houses, old men who had seen the first house, wept with a loud voice when they saw the foundation of this house being laid, though many shouted aloud for joy, so that the people could not distinguish the sound of the joyful shout from the sound of the people's weeping, for the people shouted with a great shout, and the sound was heard far away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But many of the priests and Levites and heads of fathers' houses, old men who had seen the first house, wept with a loud voice when they saw the foundation of this house being laid, though many shouted aloud for joy.

Old men who had seen the first house. Do the arithmetic: Solomon's temple was burned in 586, and this foundation is laid about fifty years later. Anyone who could remember that building standing was now in his sixties at least, and had seen it as a boy. They had walked in its courts holding a father's hand. They remembered the size of it, the gold, the bronze pillars, the crowds at the feasts.

And they could see from the foundation lines how big this one was going to be. That is what set them off. Not a vague nostalgia — a measurement. The trench was marked out on the ground in front of them, and it was smaller.

The prophet Haggai spoke to exactly these men a few years later, and he did not pretend. Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How do you see it now? Is it not as nothing in your eyes? (Hag 2:3). He granted every word of their grief.

And the young men shouted. They had been born in Babylon. They had no memory of gold on the walls to measure against; they had only the promise that God would bring his people back, and here was a foundation to prove it. For them any foundation was a miracle, and they were right too.

So that the people could not distinguish the sound of the joyful shout from the sound of the people's weeping, for the people shouted with a great shout, and the sound was heard far away.

Could not distinguish. Anyone standing a little way off heard one noise, and could not have told you whether Jerusalem was celebrating or grieving. It was doing both, at full volume, at the same time.

That is the most honest picture of the church in the whole Old Testament. Every congregation that has ever gathered has contained both sounds: people who remember better days and grieve the gap, and people who see only the grace of what God is doing now and cannot stop shouting about it. Neither is wrong. A church that only shouts has forgotten what was lost; a church that only weeps has forgotten who laid the foundation. The book does not ask either group to be quiet.

And the sound carried. The next verse begins Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard (4:1). The noise of that morning is what brought the opposition. Joy in God's work is audible a long way off, and not everyone who hears it is glad.

The old men wept because this house would be smaller than Solomon's, and Haggai answered them with a promise they could not have understood: The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former (Hag 2:9). It was. Solomon's temple had the gold and the cloud; it never had the Son of God in it. This one did. Into this house, rebuilt and enlarged but still the second house, a baby was carried to be presented, and a twelve-year-old sat among the teachers asking questions, and a grown man drove out the money-changers and said it was his Father's house. The old men mourned a building that was smaller. They had just laid the foundation of the only temple the Lord of the temple ever walked into.

4.title: The Long Delay: Opposition, Discouragement, and Silence
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the returned exiles were building a temple to the LORD, the God of Israel,<sup>2</sup>they approached Zerubbabel and the heads of fathers' houses and said to them, "Let us build with you, for we worship your God as you do, and we have been sacrificing to him ever since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assyria who brought us here."<sup>3</sup>But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the rest of the heads of fathers' houses in Israel said to them, "You have nothing to do with us in building a house to our God; but we alone will build to the LORD, the God of Israel, as King Cyrus the king of Persia has commanded us."<sup>4</sup>Then the people of the land discouraged the people of Judah and made them afraid to build<sup>5</sup>and bribed counselors against them to frustrate their purpose, all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius king of Persia.<sup>6</sup>And in the reign of Ahasuerus, in the beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem.<sup>7</sup>In the days of Artaxerxes, Bishlam and Mithredath and Tabeel and the rest of their associates wrote to Artaxerxes king of Persia. The letter was written in Aramaic and translated.<sup>8</sup>Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king as follows:<sup>9</sup>Rehum the commander, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their associates, the judges, the governors, the officials, the Persians, the men of Erech, the Babylonians, the men of Susa, that is, the Elamites,<sup>10</sup>and the rest of the nations whom the great and noble Osnappar deported and settled in the cities of Samaria and in the rest of the province Beyond the River.<sup>11</sup>(This is a copy of the letter that they sent.) "To Artaxerxes the king: Your servants, the men of the province Beyond the River, send greeting. And now<sup>12</sup>be it known to the king that the Jews who came up from you to us have gone to Jerusalem. They are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city. They are finishing the walls and repairing the foundations.<sup>13</sup>Now be it known to the king that if this city is rebuilt and the walls finished, they will not pay tribute, custom, or toll, and the royal revenue will be impaired.<sup>14</sup>Now because we eat the salt of the palace and it is not fitting for us to witness the king's dishonor, therefore we send and inform the king,<sup>15</sup>in order that search may be made in the book of the records of your fathers. You will find in the book of the records and learn that this city is a rebellious city, hurtful to kings and provinces, and that sedition was stirred up in it from of old. That was why this city was laid waste.<sup>16</sup>We make known to the king that if this city is rebuilt and its walls finished, you will then have no possession in the province Beyond the River."<sup>17</sup>The king sent an answer: "To Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe and the rest of their associates who live in Samaria and in the rest of the province Beyond the River, greeting. And now<sup>18</sup>the letter that you sent to us has been plainly read before me.<sup>19</sup>And I made a decree, and search has been made, and it has been found that this city from of old has risen against kings, and that rebellion and sedition have been made in it.<sup>20</sup>And mighty kings have been over Jerusalem, who ruled over the whole province Beyond the River, to whom tribute, custom, and toll were paid.<sup>21</sup>Therefore make a decree that these men be made to cease, and that this city be not rebuilt, until a decree is made by me.<sup>22</sup>And take care not to be slack in this matter. Why should damage grow to the hurt of the king?"<sup>23</sup>Then, when the copy of King Artaxerxes' letter was read before Rehum and Shimshai the scribe and their associates, they went in haste to the Jews at Jerusalem and by force and power made them cease.<sup>24</sup>Then the work on the house of God that is in Jerusalem stopped, and it ceased until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.
4.overview: When the adversaries hear the building, they offer to join it — we worship your God as you do — and are refused, because they are the resettled peoples of 2 Kings 17 who feared the LORD and served their own gods as well (vv. 1-3). So they weaken the builders' hands, frighten them and bribe officials against them for the rest of Cyrus's reign and into Darius's (vv. 4-5). Then the chapter leaps forward: an accusation under Xerxes (v. 6), and under Artaxerxes a letter — given in the Aramaic it was written in — warning that the Jews are rebuilding the rebellious city's walls and will stop paying tribute (vv. 7-16). The king searches, finds the charge true, and stops the work until a decree is made by me; the officials enforce it by force (vv. 17-23). Verse 24 returns to the temple: the work ceased until the second year of Darius.
4.theology:
The first opposition is an offer of help. The refusal in verse 3 is of a partnership with a mixed religion, not of people: 6:21 welcomes anyone who separates from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to worship the LORD. The test was never whether others used the name of God but whether they wanted God alone.

Verses 6-23 are arranged by theme, not date, so that ninety years of opposition can be seen whole. And the accusation that finally works is a true one: Jerusalem had rebelled. The accuser rarely needs to lie; he only reads the record aloud when God's people try to build. The answer is not denial but the verdict of Zechariah 3 and Romans 8 — the filthy garments removed, and it is God who justifies.
4.examples:
The narrator calls them adversaries before they say a single friendly word.

They admitted in their own offer that Assyria had brought them there.

Fear drove the returnees to the altar in chapter 3 and off the building site in chapter 4.

From verse 8 the book is written in Aramaic, the language of the Persian letters it quotes, and stays in it until 6:18.

The accusers' letter was accurate about Jerusalem's past, and the king's archive confirmed it — and also confirmed that mighty kings once ruled the whole region from there.

The order that stopped the walls said until a decree is made by me, and the same king later sent Nehemiah to build them.

The foundation lay in the ground for sixteen years.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Let Us Build with You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the returned exiles were building a temple (v. 1), they come to Zerubbabel with an offer: Let us build with you, for we worship your God as you do, and we have been sacrificing to him ever since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assyria who brought us here (v. 2). The answer is no: You have nothing to do with us in building a house to our God; but we alone will build ... as King Cyrus the king of Persia has commanded us (v. 3). So the people of the land weaken the builders' hands and frighten them (v. 4), and bribe officials against them all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The offer sounded like worship, and the history behind it was the one told in 2 Kings: peoples resettled in Samaria by Assyria who feared the LORD but also served their own gods (2 Kgs 17:33). What was refused was a joint building with a mixed religion, not a person who wanted God — the Passover at 6:21 welcomes every one who had joined them and separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land.
verseByVerse.examples: The most dangerous opposition in this chapter is the first, and it arrives smiling. Nobody threatens anyone in verse 2. They offer to help, and they use the right words to do it. The threats come only after the help has been declined, which tells you what the help was for.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the returned exiles were building a temple to the LORD, the God of Israel, they approached Zerubbabel and the heads of fathers' houses and said to them, "Let us build with you, for we worship your God as you do, and we have been sacrificing to him ever since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assyria who brought us here." But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the rest of the heads of fathers' houses in Israel said to them, "You have nothing to do with us in building a house to our God; but we alone will build to the LORD, the God of Israel, as King Cyrus the king of Persia has commanded us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the returned exiles were building a temple to the LORD, the God of Israel.

Heard. The last chapter ended with a sound heard far away (3:13), the shouting and weeping over the foundation, and this is who heard it. And the writer tells us what they are before they open their mouths: adversaries. Nothing in what they are about to say will sound like it.

They approached Zerubbabel and the heads of fathers' houses and said to them, Let us build with you, for we worship your God as you do, and we have been sacrificing to him ever since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assyria who brought us here.

It is a generous-sounding offer, and it contains its own history. Who brought us here. These are the descendants of the peoples Assyria planted in Samaria after it emptied the northern kingdom, brought in from Babylon, Cuthah, Hamath and elsewhere (2 Kgs 17:24). And the book of Kings describes their religion in one sentence: they feared the LORD but also served their own gods (17:33), and their children and grandchildren did the same to this day (17:41).

So when they say we worship your God as you do, it is half true, and the half that is missing is the whole point. They worshipped the LORD as one god among several. Building his house together would have meant building it as one shrine among several.

But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the rest of the heads of fathers' houses in Israel said to them, You have nothing to do with us in building a house to our God; but we alone will build to the LORD, the God of Israel, as King Cyrus the king of Persia has commanded us.

To a modern ear that sounds hard, and it needs to be read carefully, because the rest of the book tells us what it did not mean. It did not mean that nobody from outside could ever join them. Two chapters later the Passover is eaten by the returned exiles and also by every one who had joined them and separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to worship the LORD (6:21). Anyone could come in who came to the LORD alone.

What was refused was a partnership: a joint building project with a religion that kept its other gods. And the ground they give is not their own preference but the commission itself — as King Cyrus the king of Persia has commanded us. The decree was given to the people who went up. They had no authority to subcontract it.

Churches meet this offer still, and it still comes with the right vocabulary. Not every invitation to build together is an invitation to build the same thing. The test is not whether the other party uses the name of God, but whether they want God alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of the land discouraged the people of Judah and made them afraid to build and bribed counselors against them to frustrate their purpose, all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius king of Persia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The response to the refusal shows what the offer had been.

Then the people of the land discouraged the people of Judah and made them afraid to build.

The Hebrew behind discouraged is a vivid phrase: they weakened the hands of the people of Judah. Opposition aimed at the hands, at the capacity to work. Two chapters ago fear drove these people to the altar (3:3). Now fear drives them off the building site. The same emotion, and two opposite results, depending on where it was carried.

And bribed counselors against them to frustrate their purpose, all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius king of Persia.

Bribed counsellors — paid advisers at court, working the officials, year after year. This is not a mob with torches. It is a funded, patient campaign that ran from the end of Cyrus's reign into Darius's: roughly sixteen years. It worked. The foundation laid with such noise in chapter 3 sat in the ground, and nothing went up on it.

That is how most good work of God is stopped in practice. Not by a single catastrophe but by a steady pressure that makes it slightly harder every week, until the people who began it with shouting have quietly gone back to their own affairs. Haggai will arrive to tell them exactly that: they were living in panelled houses while the house of God lay in ruins (Hag 1:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–24 — Be It Known to the King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Under Ahasuerus an accusation is lodged (v. 6). Under Artaxerxes a letter is written in Aramaic (v. 7), and from verse 8 the book itself is written in Aramaic. Rehum and Shimshai tell the king that the Jews are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city and its walls (vv. 8-12); that once it is rebuilt they will not pay tribute, custom, or toll (v. 13); and that the records will prove it (vv. 14-16). The king searches, finds that the city from of old has risen against kings, and orders the work stopped until a decree is made by me (vv. 17-22). They go in haste and stop it by force and power (v. 23). Then the work on the house of God that is in Jerusalem stopped, and it ceased until the second year of the reign of Darius (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 6-23 leap forward in time. Ahasuerus is Xerxes, who reigned a generation after the temple was finished, and Artaxerxes after him; their letters concern the city wall, not the house of God. Verse 24 then steps back to the temple in Darius's day. The writer has gathered ninety years of opposition into one chapter so the reader sees the pattern whole: whenever God's people build, someone writes to the king.
verseByVerse.examples: The worst thing about the letter is that its history was accurate. Jerusalem had rebelled; its last king broke an oath sworn by God to Nebuchadnezzar (2 Chr 36:13). The accusers did not need to lie. They took Judah's real past and used it to forbid Judah's future, and the king's own research confirmed every word.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the reign of Ahasuerus, in the beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem. In the days of Artaxerxes, Bishlam and Mithredath and Tabeel and the rest of their associates wrote to Artaxerxes king of Persia. The letter was written in Aramaic and translated. Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king as follows: Rehum the commander, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their associates, the judges, the governors, the officials, the Persians, the men of Erech, the Babylonians, the men of Susa, that is, the Elamites, and the rest of the nations whom the great and noble Osnappar deported and settled in the cities of Samaria and in the rest of the province Beyond the River. (This is a copy of the letter that they sent.) "To Artaxerxes the king: Your servants, the men of the province Beyond the River, send greeting. And now be it known to the king that the Jews who came up from you to us have gone to Jerusalem. They are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city. They are finishing the walls and repairing the foundations. Now be it known to the king that if this city is rebuilt and the walls finished, they will not pay tribute, custom, or toll, and the royal revenue will be impaired.
