Now because we eat the salt of the palace and it is not fitting for us to witness the king's dishonor, therefore we send and inform the king, in order that search may be made in the book of the records of your fathers. You will find in the book of the records and learn that this city is a rebellious city, hurtful to kings and provinces, and that sedition was stirred up in it from of old. That was why this city was laid waste. We make known to the king that if this city is rebuilt and its walls finished, you will then have no possession in the province Beyond the River."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the chapter does something a careful reader must notice, or the rest of it will not make sense. It jumps forward in time.

And in the reign of Ahasuerus, in the beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem. Ahasuerus is Xerxes, the king of the book of Esther, who came to the throne about thirty years after the temple was finished. Then verse 7: In the days of Artaxerxes — his son, later still. And what the Artaxerxes letter complains about is not the temple but the city: they are finishing the walls and repairing the foundations.

The writer is not confused about the order of the Persian kings. He has gathered opposition from ninety years into one chapter to show the reader that it was not an incident but a pattern. Whenever the people of God began to build anything in Jerusalem — the temple under Darius, the walls under Artaxerxes — somebody wrote to the king. Verse 24 will step back to the temple and pick up the thread from verse 5.

Verse 7 adds a detail that an English reader cannot see: The letter was written in Aramaic and translated. From verse 8 onward, the book itself is written in Aramaic, the language of the Persian chancery, and it does not return to Hebrew until 6:18. The letters are given in the language they were sent in.

The letter itself is a small masterpiece. It opens by listing everyone who signed it — officials, judges, Persians, men of Erech and Babylon and Susa, all the nations whom the great and noble Osnappar deported — so that the king sees a whole province of loyal subjects on one side and a few Jews on the other.

Then it goes for the purse. If this city is rebuilt and the walls finished, they will not pay tribute, custom, or toll, and the royal revenue will be impaired. Then it wraps the purse in loyalty: because we eat the salt of the palace — we are on your payroll, and we cannot bear to see you dishonoured.

And then the clever part. Search may be made in the book of the records of your fathers. You will find ... that this city is a rebellious city.

That is the worst thing about this letter: it was true. Jerusalem had rebelled. Its last king broke an oath he had sworn by God to Nebuchadnezzar (2 Chr 36:13), and the city was burned for it. The accusers did not have to invent anything. They took Judah's real past and used it to forbid Judah's future.

There is an accuser who works the same way. He rarely needs to lie about a believer's history. He only needs to read it out, accurately, at the moment the believer is trying to build something for God, and suggest that people with a record like that should not be allowed to start again.

verseByVerse.quote: The king sent an answer: "To Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe and the rest of their associates who live in Samaria and in the rest of the province Beyond the River, greeting. And now the letter that you sent to us has been plainly read before me. And I made a decree, and search has been made, and it has been found that this city from of old has risen against kings, and that rebellion and sedition have been made in it. And mighty kings have been over Jerusalem, who ruled over the whole province Beyond the River, to whom tribute, custom, and toll were paid. Therefore make a decree that these men be made to cease, and that this city be not rebuilt, until a decree is made by me. And take care not to be slack in this matter. Why should damage grow to the hurt of the king?" Then, when the copy of King Artaxerxes' letter was read before Rehum and Shimshai the scribe and their associates, they went in haste to the Jews at Jerusalem and by force and power made them cease.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king does what he was asked. Search has been made, and it has been found that this city from of old has risen against kings, and that rebellion and sedition have been made in it.

And then, in the middle of the royal reply, a sentence the accusers can hardly have wanted: And mighty kings have been over Jerusalem, who ruled over the whole province Beyond the River, to whom tribute, custom, and toll were paid. The Persian archives remember David and Solomon. The emperor's own records confirm that this ruined little town once governed the whole region from the Euphrates to Egypt. The search meant to condemn Jerusalem turned up evidence of its glory as well.

Therefore make a decree that these men be made to cease, and that this city be not rebuilt, until a decree is made by me.

Until a decree is made by me. Keep hold of that clause, because it is a door the king left open without meaning to. Some years later the same Artaxerxes will look at his cupbearer's sad face across a wine cup, ask what is wrong, and give Nehemiah letters to rebuild these very walls (Neh 2:1-8). The decree that stopped the work contained the words that would one day restart it.

Then, when the copy of King Artaxerxes' letter was read before Rehum and Shimshai the scribe and their associates, they went in haste to the Jews at Jerusalem and by force and power made them cease.

In haste, and by force. They did not wait for the dispatch to be formally delivered; they rode to Jerusalem and pulled the workmen off the walls. That broken wall is very likely the one Nehemiah heard about in Susa, which made him sit down and weep (Neh 1:3-4).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the work on the house of God that is in Jerusalem stopped, and it ceased until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the work on the house of God that is in Jerusalem stopped, and it ceased until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.

With this verse the writer steps back from Artaxerxes' reign to the story he left at verse 5. The subject is the house of God again, and the date is fixed: nothing more was built on it until Darius's second year, 520 BC. From the laying of the foundation, that is about sixteen years.

Sixteen years. A child born the week the foundation was laid was a teenager before another stone went up. The altar still smoked morning and evening; the foundation lay in the ground with weeds growing in the trench. The people who had shouted over it got on with their farms.

This is one of the most honest verses in the Old Testament for anyone who has given years to a work of God that stalled. The Bible does not pretend that opposition always fails quickly or that faithful people are never stopped. It records sixteen years of nothing, and does not hurry past them.

But it records them with an end date. Until the second year of the reign of Darius. The stoppage was real, and it was not permanent, and the God who let it happen had already decided when it would end.

And the accusation of verse 15 was answered, in the end, not by proving it false but by God himself. The prophet Zechariah, who is about to appear in the next chapter, saw in a vision Jeshua the high priest — the same man who built the altar in chapter 3 — standing before the angel of the LORD in filthy clothes, and Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him. The accusation was true; the clothes were filthy. And the LORD said, The LORD rebuke you, O Satan! ... Is not this a brand plucked from the fire? — and ordered the filthy garments taken off and clean ones put on (Zech 3:1-5).

That is still how the charge sheet is dealt with. Not by arguing that the record is exaggerated, but by the One who has taken the record away. Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died ... who indeed is interceding for us (Rom 8:33-34).

5.title: The Prophets Arise: Haggai, Zechariah, and the Resumption of Work
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the prophets, Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied to the Jews who were in Judah and Jerusalem, in the name of the God of Israel who was over them.<sup>2</sup>Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak arose and began to rebuild the house of God that is in Jerusalem, and the prophets of God were with them, supporting them.<sup>3</sup>At the same time Tattenai the governor of the province Beyond the River and Shethar-bozenai and their associates came to them and spoke to them thus: "Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this structure?"<sup>4</sup>They also asked them this: "What are the names of the men who are building this building?"<sup>5</sup>But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, and they did not stop them until the report should reach Darius and then an answer be returned by letter concerning it.<sup>6</sup>This is a copy of the letter that Tattenai the governor of the province Beyond the River and Shethar-bozenai and his associates, the governors who were in the province Beyond the River, sent to Darius the king.<sup>7</sup>They sent him a report, in which was written as follows: "To Darius the king, all peace.<sup>8</sup>Be it known to the king that we went to the province of Judah, to the house of the great God. It is being built with huge stones, and timber is laid in the walls. This work goes on diligently and prospers in their hands.<sup>9</sup>Then we asked those elders and spoke to them thus: 'Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this structure?'<sup>10</sup>We also asked them their names, for your information, that we might write down the names of their leaders.<sup>11</sup>And this was their reply to us: 'We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the house that was built many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and finished.<sup>12</sup>But because our fathers had angered the God of heaven, he gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean, who destroyed this house and carried away the people to Babylonia.<sup>13</sup>However, in the first year of Cyrus king of Babylon, Cyrus the king made a decree that this house of God should be rebuilt.<sup>14</sup>And the gold and silver vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken out of the temple that was in Jerusalem and brought into the temple of Babylon, these Cyrus the king took out of the temple of Babylon, and they were delivered to one whose name was Sheshbazzar, whom he had made governor;<sup>15</sup>and he said to him, "Take these vessels, go and put them in the temple that is in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be rebuilt on its site."<sup>16</sup>Then this Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundations of the house of God that is in Jerusalem, and from that time until now it has been in building, and it is not yet finished.'<sup>17</sup>Therefore, if it seems good to the king, let search be made in the royal archives there in Babylon, to see whether a decree was issued by Cyrus the king for the rebuilding of this house of God in Jerusalem. And let the king send us his pleasure in this matter."
5.overview: After sixteen idle years, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah preach, and Zerubbabel and Jeshua rise up and start building, with the prophets beside them (vv. 1-2) — twenty-three days, by Haggai's dates, from his first sermon to the first stone (Hag 1:1, 15). At once the governor Tattenai comes asking who authorised it and who the builders are, but the eye of their God was on the elders, and the work goes on while the question goes to Darius (vv. 3-5). Tattenai's report is fair: a great house of huge stones, a work prospering in their hands (vv. 6-10). The elders' answer is honest to the point of confession — we are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and the first house fell because our fathers had angered the God of heaven — followed by Cyrus's decree, the returned vessels, and a request that the archives be searched (vv. 11-17).
5.theology:
The work of God restarts when the word of God is preached. Nothing in the political situation changed between chapter 4 and chapter 5; two prophets spoke, and Haggai describes the result with Ezra's own verb — the LORD stirred up the spirit of the leaders and all the remnant (Hag 1:14). The God who stirred an emperor by providence stirred his people by a sermon.

Verse 5 is watchfulness without guarantee: the builders did not know how Darius would answer, and they worked on under the eye of their God. And verse 12 shows the only safe way to hold a guilty past — confess it plainly. The accusers of chapter 4 had used Jerusalem's history as a weapon; here the builders name their fathers' sin themselves, and there is nothing left to use against them.
5.examples:
Haggai's first sermon was on the first of the month; the work restarted on the twenty-fourth.

His whole second oracle was one sentence: I am with you, declares the LORD.

The prophets did not preach and leave; they were on the building site, supporting the men they had rebuked.

The governor who came to investigate reported that the work was going on diligently and prospering.

The builders kept working for the weeks it took a letter to reach the king and come back.

Asked why their temple had been destroyed, they told a Persian official it was their own fathers' fault.

A trench full of weeds for sixteen years was described to the governor as the house being in building.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Eye of Their God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the prophets, Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied to the Jews who were in Judah and Jerusalem, in the name of the God of Israel who was over them (v. 1). Then Zerubbabel ... and Jeshua ... arose and began to rebuild, and the prophets were with them, supporting them (v. 2). At once Tattenai the governor and his colleagues arrive: Who gave you a decree to build this house? (v. 3), and what are the builders' names? (v. 4). But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, and they did not stop them until Darius could answer (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Sixteen years of nothing end in two verses, and what ends them is preaching. Haggai dated his first sermon to the first day of the sixth month (Hag 1:1), and on the twenty-fourth of the same month the people were back on the site — and Haggai uses the verb of Ezra's first chapter: the LORD stirred up the spirit of the governor, the high priest and all the remnant (Hag 1:14-15). The same God who stirred Cyrus stirred them again, and this time he did it through a sermon.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 is the chapter's comfort. The inquiry was real and the builders had no idea how it would end, and they kept working while it was pending, because the eye of their God was on the elders. It is the watchfulness the seer Hanani described to Asa: the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him (2 Chr 16:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the prophets, Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied to the Jews who were in Judah and Jerusalem, in the name of the God of Israel who was over them. Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak arose and began to rebuild the house of God that is in Jerusalem, and the prophets of God were with them, supporting them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the prophets, Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied to the Jews who were in Judah and Jerusalem, in the name of the God of Israel who was over them.

Sixteen years of silence end with two preachers. Nothing else in the situation had changed. The officials who had frightened the builders were still there, the bribed counsellors were still on the payroll, the foundation was still sitting in its trench with the weeds in it. What changed was that God spoke.

We have Haggai's sermons, and they are not gentle. Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins? (Hag 1:4). The people had told themselves that the time was not yet right (Hag 1:2); Haggai pointed out that the time had been right enough for their own carpentry. Poor harvests, wages that ran through a bag with holes in it — he told them to consider their ways.

And then the dates, which Haggai supplies to the day. His first message came on the first day of the sixth month of Darius's second year (Hag 1:1). Between that sermon and the next there is one sentence from God, the shortest oracle in the prophets: I am with you, declares the LORD (Hag 1:13). And on the twenty-fourth day of the same month, the work began (Hag 1:15). Twenty-three days from the first sermon to the first stone.

Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak arose and began to rebuild the house of God that is in Jerusalem, and the prophets of God were with them, supporting them.

Haggai describes the same moment with the verb of this book's first chapter: the LORD stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel ... and the spirit of Joshua ... and the spirit of all the remnant of the people. And they came and worked on the house (Hag 1:14). The God who stirred Cyrus to write a decree and stirred the families to leave Babylon stirred them a third time, and this time he did it by a sermon.

And the preachers did not go home after preaching. The prophets of God were with them, supporting them. They were on the site. Whatever supporting meant in practice — encouragement, further oracles, perhaps their own hands on the ropes — Haggai and Zechariah stood with the men they had rebuked while the men did what they had been told.

That is still how God restarts stalled work. Not usually by a change of circumstances, but by a word, plainly spoken, that tells people what they already half know, and a God who stays beside them after they obey it.

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time Tattenai the governor of the province Beyond the River and Shethar-bozenai and their associates came to them and spoke to them thus: "Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this structure?" They also asked them this: "What are the names of the men who are building this building?" But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, and they did not stop them until the report should reach Darius and then an answer be returned by letter concerning it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the same time Tattenai the governor of the province Beyond the River and Shethar-bozenai and their associates came to them.

The timing is pointed. The builders had been at it for perhaps a few weeks when the regional governor arrived. After chapter 4 the reader braces for another round of accusation, and the question he asks sounds like it: Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this structure? And then, more ominously, What are the names of the men who are building this building? Writing down names is what officials do before arrests.

But it is a fair question. Tattenai governs a province for the Persian crown; a large building going up on the site of a city with a history of revolt is exactly the sort of thing he is paid to ask about. His name, as it happens, turns up in a Babylonian document of Darius's reign with the same title. He is a real civil servant doing a real job.

But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, and they did not stop them until the report should reach Darius and then an answer be returned by letter concerning it.

The eye of their God. They did not know how the inquiry would come out. The last time letters went to a Persian king about Jerusalem, the work was stopped by force. And they kept building while the letter travelled, which was weeks each way at least, because the one watching them was not Tattenai.

The seer Hanani once told Asa that the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him (2 Chr 16:9). Here that is, in the form of a provincial governor who decided, for reasons of his own, not to issue a stop order.

Anyone waiting on a decision they cannot control — a hearing, a result, a letter that could go either way — can take this verse personally. The outcome was not yet known. The eye was already on them. They went on working.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–17 — We Are the Servants of the God of Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tattenai's report to Darius is fair. He describes the house of the great God, built with huge stones and timber, a work that goes on diligently and prospers in their hands (vv. 6-8). He records his questions (vv. 9-10) and their answer: We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the house that was built many years ago (v. 11). But because our fathers had angered the God of heaven, he gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar (v. 12). Cyrus decreed the rebuilding, returned the vessels, and sent Sheshbazzar, who laid the foundations, and from that time until now it has been in building, and it is not yet finished (vv. 13-16). So let the king search the archives in Babylon (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Asked by a Persian official why their temple had been destroyed, the elders did not blame Babylon. They said their fathers had angered God, and God had handed them over. The accusers of chapter 4 had called Jerusalem a rebellious city; the builders went further than their accusers and named the real offence themselves. A people who can tell the truth about their own sin cannot be blackmailed with it.
verseByVerse.examples: Tattenai is not the villain the reader expects after chapter 4. He asks the right question, lets the work continue while he asks it, describes the building accurately and even admiringly, and asks the king to check the builders' claim rather than his own suspicions. An honest official is a gift of God, and the text takes the trouble to show us one.

verseByVerse.quote: This is a copy of the letter that Tattenai the governor of the province Beyond the River and Shethar-bozenai and his associates, the governors who were in the province Beyond the River, sent to Darius the king. They sent him a report, in which was written as follows: "To Darius the king, all peace. Be it known to the king that we went to the province of Judah, to the house of the great God. It is being built with huge stones, and timber is laid in the walls. This work goes on diligently and prospers in their hands. Then we asked those elders and spoke to them thus: 'Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this structure?' We also asked them their names, for your information, that we might write down the names of their leaders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then comes a copy of Tattenai's report to the king, and the surprise is how fair it is.

To Darius the king, all peace. Be it known to the king that we went to the province of Judah, to the house of the great God. It is being built with huge stones, and timber is laid in the walls. This work goes on diligently and prospers in their hands.

Compare it with the letter of chapter 4. That one called Jerusalem that rebellious and wicked city, went straight for the king's tax revenue and demanded action. This one calls the building the house of the great God, describes the masonry, and reports that the work is going well — diligently, prospering in their hands. It is the sort of description a sympathetic observer might give.

He records what he asked and why. We also asked them their names, for your information, that we might write down the names of their leaders. For your information: this is a file, not a charge.

Not every questioner is an enemy. After a chapter of opposition, a person can learn to hear every enquiry as an attack and every official as Rehum the commander. The book will not let us do that. Tattenai asked hard questions honestly and wrote down the answers straight, and God used his fairness as surely as he used the prophets' sermons.

verseByVerse.quote: And this was their reply to us: 'We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the house that was built many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and finished. But because our fathers had angered the God of heaven, he gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean, who destroyed this house and carried away the people to Babylonia. However, in the first year of Cyrus king of Babylon, Cyrus the king made a decree that this house of God should be rebuilt. And the gold and silver vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken out of the temple that was in Jerusalem and brought into the temple of Babylon, these Cyrus the king took out of the temple of Babylon, and they were delivered to one whose name was Sheshbazzar, whom he had made governor; and he said to him, "Take these vessels, go and put them in the temple that is in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be rebuilt on its site." Then this Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundations of the house of God that is in Jerusalem, and from that time until now it has been in building, and it is not yet finished.' Therefore, if it seems good to the king, let search be made in the royal archives there in Babylon, to see whether a decree was issued by Cyrus the king for the rebuilding of this house of God in Jerusalem. And let the king send us his pleasure in this matter."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders' reply, as Tattenai records it, is a small sermon in its own right.

We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the house that was built many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and finished.

The first thing they say about themselves is servants. Not Judeans, not subjects of Persia, not the Zerubbabel party. Servants of the God who made heaven and earth — which is a large claim to make to the governor of a province, and they make it before they mention anybody's decree.

Then they tell him why the first house is not standing, and they do not spare themselves. But because our fathers had angered the God of heaven, he gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean, who destroyed this house and carried away the people to Babylonia.

Set that beside chapter 4. The accusers wrote to Artaxerxes that Jerusalem was a rebellious city, and the charge worked because it was true. Here the builders are asked the same history, and they go further than their accusers ever did: it was not Babylon's doing, and not bad luck, and not even simply rebellion against a king. Our fathers angered God, and God handed them over.

That is the only safe way to hold a guilty past. A people who will tell the truth about their own sin, out loud, to a stranger, cannot be blackmailed with it. The accuser's leverage is always the thing we are hiding, and they had stopped hiding it.

Then the good news, in order: Cyrus decreed the rebuilding; Cyrus returned the vessels and gave them to Sheshbazzar; Sheshbazzar laid the foundations — and from that time until now it has been in building, and it is not yet finished.

That last clause is a kindly way of describing sixteen years of weeds in a trench. Haggai, a few weeks earlier, had put it rather differently: These people say the time has not yet come to rebuild the house of the LORD (Hag 1:2). The elders did not lie to Tattenai — the building had been begun and not abandoned in law — but they chose their words with care, as people generally do when talking to a governor.

And they end by inviting the check. Let search be made in the royal archives there in Babylon, to see whether a decree was issued by Cyrus the king. In chapter 4 the archive was a weapon, searched to prove Jerusalem guilty. Here it is asked for by the people with nothing to hide.

They built on, not knowing what the search would find, with nothing to rest on but a decree they could not produce and a promise from Haggai that fitted into one line: I am with you, declares the LORD. It is the same promise the Lord Jesus gave to the church when he sent it out to build something far larger than a temple, with no decree it could show the world's governors except his word: And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matt 28:20).

6.title: The Temple Completed: Darius's Decree, Dedication, and Passover
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Darius the king made a decree, and search was made in Babylonia, in the house of the archives where the documents were stored.<sup>2</sup>And in Ecbatana, the citadel that is in the province of Media, a scroll was found on which this was written: "A record.<sup>3</sup>In the first year of Cyrus the king, Cyrus the king issued a decree: Concerning the house of God at Jerusalem, let the house be rebuilt, the place where sacrifices were offered, and let its foundations be retained. Its height shall be sixty cubits and its breadth sixty cubits,<sup>4</sup>with three layers of great stones and one layer of timber. Let the cost be paid from the royal treasury.<sup>5</sup>And also let the gold and silver vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took out of the temple that is in Jerusalem and brought to Babylon, be restored and brought back to the temple that is in Jerusalem, each to its place. You shall put them in the house of God."<sup>6</sup>"Now therefore, Tattenai, governor of the province Beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai, and your associates the governors who are in the province Beyond the River, keep away.<sup>7</sup>Let the work on this house of God alone. Let the governor of the Jews and the elders of the Jews rebuild this house of God on its site.<sup>8</sup>Moreover, I make a decree regarding what you shall do for these elders of the Jews for the rebuilding of this house of God. The cost is to be paid to these men in full and without delay from the royal revenue, the tribute of the province from Beyond the River.<sup>9</sup>And whatever is needed—bulls, rams, or sheep for burnt offerings to the God of heaven, wheat, salt, wine, or oil, as the priests at Jerusalem require—let that be given to them day by day without fail,<sup>10</sup>that they may offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons.<sup>11</sup>Also I make a decree that if anyone alters this edict, a beam shall be pulled out of his house, and he shall be impaled on it, and his house shall be made a dunghill.<sup>12</sup>May the God who has caused his name to dwell there overthrow any king or people who shall put out a hand to alter this, or to destroy this house of God that is in Jerusalem. I Darius make a decree; let it be done with all diligence."<sup>13</sup>Then, according to the word sent by Darius the king, Tattenai, the governor of the province Beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates did with all diligence what Darius the king had ordered.<sup>14</sup>And the elders of the Jews built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo. They finished their building by decree of the God of Israel and by decree of Cyrus and Darius and Artaxerxes king of Persia;<sup>15</sup>and this house was finished on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of Darius the king.<sup>16</sup>And the people of Israel, the priests and the Levites, and the rest of the returned exiles, celebrated the dedication of this house of God with joy.<sup>17</sup>They offered at the dedication of this house of God 100 bulls, 200 rams, 400 lambs, and as a sin offering for all Israel 12 male goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel.<sup>18</sup>And they set the priests in their divisions and the Levites in their divisions, for the service of God at Jerusalem, as it is written in the Book of Moses.<sup>19</sup>On the fourteenth day of the first month, the returned exiles kept the Passover.<sup>20</sup>For the priests and the Levites had purified themselves together; all of them were clean. So they slaughtered the Passover lamb for all the returned exiles, for their fellow priests, and for themselves.<sup>21</sup>It was eaten by the people of Israel who had returned from exile, and also by every one who had joined them and separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to worship the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>22</sup>And they kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days with joy, for the LORD had made them joyful and had turned the heart of the king of Assyria to them, so that he aided them in the work of the house of God, the God of Israel.
6.overview: Darius has the archives searched, and Cyrus's memorandum turns up not in Babylon but in Ecbatana: rebuild the house on its foundations, at royal expense, and return the vessels each to its place (vv. 1-5). Darius tells Tattenai to keep away, pays the builders from the province's own tribute, supplies the daily offerings so that the priests will pray for the king, and seals the edict with a blessing in Deuteronomy's language (vv. 6-12). The elders build and prosper through the prophesying of Haggai ... and Zechariah, and the house is finished in Darius's sixth year, some seventy years after the fire (vv. 13-15). It is dedicated with joy and a sin offering of twelve goats for the twelve tribes (vv. 16-18), and the Passover is kept on the right date with every priest and Levite clean, open to anyone who had left the uncleanness of the peoples of the land — for the LORD had made them joyful (vv. 19-22).
6.theology:
The chapter is a sequence of reversals, all of them God's. The archive the accusers invoked to prove Jerusalem guilty produces the decree that authorises it; the tribute they feared losing pays for the house; the empire whose ancestors began the exile — the king of Assyria — funds the altar. The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD (Prov 21:1).

And the writer credits the finished building not to Darius's money but to the prophesying of Haggai ... and Zechariah (v. 14). God's decree is named before the three kings'. The Passover that follows answers the refusal of chapter 4: the door was shut to a partnership with other gods and open to every person who left them to worship the LORD (v. 21).
6.examples:
They searched Babylon for the decree and found it three hundred miles away in a summer palace.

The tribute the accusers said Jerusalem would stop paying was spent on Jerusalem's temple.

A Persian emperor asked the Jews to pray for his life and his sons.

Solomon dedicated his house with 22,000 oxen; the returnees dedicated theirs with a hundred bulls, and made no apology.

A community from two tribes offered twelve goats, one for every tribe of Israel.

The Aramaic section of the book ends at the Passover, and the story goes back into Hebrew.

This time, every priest and Levite was clean for the feast.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Darius orders a search, and in the end the document turns up not in Babylon but in Ecbatana, the citadel that is in the province of Media (vv. 1-2): a memorandum of Cyrus's first year — rebuild the house on its foundations, to these dimensions, let the cost be paid from the royal treasury, and put the vessels back each to its place (vv. 3-5). So Darius writes to Tattenai: keep away. Let the work on this house of God alone (vv. 6-7). More than that — pay the builders in full from the tribute of the province, supply the offerings day by day, that they may offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons (vv. 8-10). Whoever alters the edict is to be impaled on a beam from his own house (v. 11), and may the God who has caused his name to dwell there overthrow anyone who touches it (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 8 pays for the house out of the tribute of the province from Beyond the River. That is the very revenue the accusers of chapter 4 warned the king he would lose if Jerusalem were rebuilt (4:13). The money their letter was meant to protect is now spent, by royal order, on the thing their letter was meant to stop.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 12 has a Persian emperor praying in the language of Deuteronomy: the God who has caused his name to dwell there is Moses' phrase for the place God would choose (Deut 12:11). Somebody in that chancery had heard it from the Jews, and the king signed it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Darius the king made a decree, and search was made in Babylonia, in the house of the archives where the documents were stored. And in Ecbatana, the citadel that is in the province of Media, a scroll was found on which this was written: "A record. In the first year of Cyrus the king, Cyrus the king issued a decree: Concerning the house of God at Jerusalem, let the house be rebuilt, the place where sacrifices were offered, and let its foundations be retained. Its height shall be sixty cubits and its breadth sixty cubits, with three layers of great stones and one layer of timber. Let the cost be paid from the royal treasury. And also let the gold and silver vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took out of the temple that is in Jerusalem and brought to Babylon, be restored and brought back to the temple that is in Jerusalem, each to its place. You shall put them in the house of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Darius the king made a decree, and search was made in Babylonia, in the house of the archives where the documents were stored. And in Ecbatana, the citadel that is in the province of Media, a scroll was found.

Tattenai had asked the king to look in Babylon (5:17), and they looked in Babylon, and it was not there. It turned up three hundred miles away in Ecbatana, the old Median capital, where the Persian kings spent their summers. Someone had filed it there in Cyrus's first year and nobody had touched it since.

That is how providence often works: not by a voice from heaven but by a clerk who kept the archive properly, and a search that went on after the obvious place came up empty.

And what they found was not the proclamation of chapter 1 but the file copy: A record. The public announcement had spoken of the God of heaven and invited volunteers. The office memorandum adds what a treasury wants to know. Let the house be rebuilt, the place where sacrifices were offered, and let its foundations be retained. Dimensions, sixty cubits by sixty. Three layers of great stones and one layer of timber. And the line that mattered most in Darius's court: Let the cost be paid from the royal treasury.

Then the vessels again: be restored and brought back to the temple that is in Jerusalem, each to its place. Each to its place. Cyrus's clerks had not only counted them out; they had minuted that every basin was to go back where it came from.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore, Tattenai, governor of the province Beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai, and your associates the governors who are in the province Beyond the River, keep away. Let the work on this house of God alone. Let the governor of the Jews and the elders of the Jews rebuild this house of God on its site. Moreover, I make a decree regarding what you shall do for these elders of the Jews for the rebuilding of this house of God. The cost is to be paid to these men in full and without delay from the royal revenue, the tribute of the province from Beyond the River. And whatever is needed—bulls, rams, or sheep for burnt offerings to the God of heaven, wheat, salt, wine, or oil, as the priests at Jerusalem require—let that be given to them day by day without fail, that they may offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons. Also I make a decree that if anyone alters this edict, a beam shall be pulled out of his house, and he shall be impaled on it, and his house shall be made a dunghill. May the God who has caused his name to dwell there overthrow any king or people who shall put out a hand to alter this, or to destroy this house of God that is in Jerusalem. I Darius make a decree; let it be done with all diligence."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Darius's reply to Tattenai goes far beyond what anyone had asked for.

Now therefore, Tattenai ... keep away. Let the work on this house of God alone. Let the governor of the Jews and the elders of the Jews rebuild this house of God on its site.

Keep away. The governor who came to ask questions is told to stand back from the site. And then Darius adds his own decree on top of Cyrus's: The cost is to be paid to these men in full and without delay from the royal revenue, the tribute of the province from Beyond the River.

The tribute of the province. Turn back to the letter the accusers wrote in chapter 4: if this city is rebuilt ... they will not pay tribute, custom, or toll, and the royal revenue will be impaired (4:13). The revenue they were so anxious to protect is now paid out, by royal order, to build the very thing they were trying to stop.

And not only the building. Whatever is needed — bulls, rams, or sheep for burnt offerings to the God of heaven, wheat, salt, wine, or oil, as the priests at Jerusalem require — let that be given to them day by day without fail. The empire is now supplying the altar's daily ration.

And the reason: that they may offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons. A Persian emperor wants the prayers of the Jews. It is exactly what Jeremiah told the first exiles to do in Babylon: seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf (Jer 29:7). Paul will tell the church the same about kings and all in authority (1 Tim 2:1-2). God's people have always been asked to pray for rulers who did not share their faith, and here a ruler asked for it himself.

The penalty clause is savage — anyone who alters the edict is to be impaled on a beam pulled from his own house — and it is Darius's, not God's. Persian kings did such things. The text records it without comment.

But the closing blessing is remarkable. May the God who has caused his name to dwell there overthrow any king or people who shall put out a hand to alter this. That is Deuteronomy's phrase — the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there (Deut 12:11) — in the mouth of a Persian king. Somebody in the chancery had learned it from the Jews, and the emperor put his seal to it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — The LORD Had Made Them Joyful
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tattenai obeys with all diligence (v. 13). And the elders of the Jews built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah, finishing the house by decree of the God of Israel and by decree of Cyrus and Darius and Artaxerxes (v. 14), on the third day of Adar in Darius's sixth year (v. 15). They dedicate it with joy (v. 16): a hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs, and a sin offering of 12 male goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel (v. 17). The priests and Levites are set in their divisions (v. 18). On the fourteenth of the first month they keep the Passover (v. 19), every priest and Levite clean (v. 20), and it is eaten by the returned exiles and also by every one who had joined them and separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land (v. 21). And they kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days with joy, for the LORD had made them joyful (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The house was burned in 586 and finished in 516 or 515 — some seventy years. Scripture itself counts the seventy more than one way: Jeremiah measured it as Babylon's dominion (Jer 25:11; 29:10), and Zechariah, preaching while this house was going up, spoke of God's anger on Jerusalem these seventy years (Zech 1:12). Either way, the God who named the number was still keeping it.
verseByVerse.examples: Twelve goats for twelve tribes, offered by a community drawn almost entirely from two of them. Hezekiah, a century and a half earlier, offered seven (2 Chr 29:21). The returnees would not shrink Israel to the size of those who had come home; they made atonement for all of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then, according to the word sent by Darius the king, Tattenai, the governor of the province Beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates did with all diligence what Darius the king had ordered. And the elders of the Jews built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo. They finished their building by decree of the God of Israel and by decree of Cyrus and Darius and Artaxerxes king of Persia; and this house was finished on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of Darius the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then, according to the word sent by Darius the king, Tattenai ... did with all diligence what Darius the king had ordered. The fair official of chapter 5 does his duty promptly.

And the elders of the Jews built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo.

Through the prophesying. The writer has just printed two imperial decrees and a treasury order, and when he says what the building actually rose on, he names two preachers. The money came from Darius. The stones came from the quarries. The house was built through the word of God.

They finished their building by decree of the God of Israel and by decree of Cyrus and Darius and Artaxerxes king of Persia. God's decree is first, and the three kings follow it. Artaxerxes had not been born when this house was finished; his name is added because in the next chapter he will send gold and silver to beautify the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem (7:27). The writer lists every king who served the house, in whatever order they came.

And this house was finished on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of Darius the king.

The sixth year of Darius is 516 or 515. Solomon's house was burned in 586. Some seventy years, then, from the fire to the finished house — and the prophets reckoned the seventy years more than one way. Jeremiah spoke of seventy years of Babylon's rule (Jer 25:11; 29:10); Zechariah, preaching on this building site, asked how long God would be angry with Jerusalem these seventy years (Zech 1:12). The number God had named came due in the time God had named, and the house stood at the end of it.

From the first stone to the last, counting the sixteen idle years, it had taken about twenty-one. From Haggai's first sermon, four and a half.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel, the priests and the Levites, and the rest of the returned exiles, celebrated the dedication of this house of God with joy. They offered at the dedication of this house of God 100 bulls, 200 rams, 400 lambs, and as a sin offering for all Israel 12 male goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel. And they set the priests in their divisions and the Levites in their divisions, for the service of God at Jerusalem, as it is written in the Book of Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the people of Israel, the priests and the Levites, and the rest of the returned exiles, celebrated the dedication of this house of God with joy.

With joy. Some of the old men who wept over the foundation twenty-one years earlier were surely dead by now. Their grandchildren stood in the finished courts, and nobody is recorded as weeping.

They offered at the dedication of this house of God 100 bulls, 200 rams, 400 lambs, and as a sin offering for all Israel 12 male goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel.

A hundred bulls. At the dedication of Solomon's house, the king offered 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep (2 Chr 7:5). The returnees did not pretend to be Solomon. They offered what a small, poor community could offer, and the writer records it without apology.

But look at the twelve goats. The community that came home was drawn almost entirely from Judah and Benjamin, and it offered a sin offering for every tribe of Israel, one goat each. Hezekiah's great sin offering was seven goats (2 Chr 29:21). These people had every reason to think of themselves as the remnant of a remnant, and they would not let Israel shrink to their own size. They made atonement for the whole people, including the ten tribes scattered by Assyria two centuries earlier.

Then the priests and Levites are set in their divisions as it is written in the Book of Moses. And with that verse, the Aramaic section of the book ends. From 4:8 to 6:18 the story has been told in the language of the Persian letters. At verse 19 it returns to Hebrew — at the Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: On the fourteenth day of the first month, the returned exiles kept the Passover. For the priests and the Levites had purified themselves together; all of them were clean. So they slaughtered the Passover lamb for all the returned exiles, for their fellow priests, and for themselves. It was eaten by the people of Israel who had returned from exile, and also by every one who had joined them and separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to worship the LORD, the God of Israel. And they kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days with joy, for the LORD had made them joyful and had turned the heart of the king of Assyria to them, so that he aided them in the work of the house of God, the God of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the fourteenth day of the first month, the returned exiles kept the Passover.

On the right date. A reader who has just come through 2 Chronicles will remember that Hezekiah had to move his Passover to the second month, because the priests had not consecrated themselves in sufficient number (2 Chr 30:3), and that at the feast itself many were unclean and the Levites had to kill the lambs for them.

For the priests and the Levites had purified themselves together; all of them were clean. All of them. Not one priest unready, not one Levite short. The first Passover in the rebuilt house is the one where the clergy had dealt with themselves in good time.

It was eaten by the people of Israel who had returned from exile, and also by every one who had joined them and separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to worship the LORD, the God of Israel.

Here is the verse that tells us how to read the refusal of chapter 4. The door was never shut to people. Anyone from the peoples of the land who turned from their gods to the LORD could sit down to this meal, exactly as the law had provided for the stranger at the first Passover in Egypt (Exod 12:48). What was refused in chapter 4 was a partnership with other gods. What is welcomed here is a person who has left them.

And they kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days with joy, for the LORD had made them joyful and had turned the heart of the king of Assyria to them, so that he aided them in the work of the house of God.

The LORD had made them joyful. Their joy is given, like everything else in this book: the spirits stirred in chapter 1, the sermons of chapter 5, the scroll in Ecbatana. The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will (Prov 21:1), and he had turned it.

Notice too that Darius is called the king of Assyria. It is an old title for the power that ruled that empire's lands, and it names the kingdom whose armies began Israel's exile, carrying the northern tribes away two centuries before. The empire that started the scattering is now paying for the altar. The circle has closed.

The first half of Ezra ends with a lamb killed and eaten by a people who had come home, and with foreigners who had turned to God at the same table. It is the right place for it to end. Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Cor 5:7), and the table he keeps is the same shape: exiles brought home, strangers who have left their gods, and a joy that nobody at it manufactured.

7.title: The Scribe-Priest Arrives: Ezra, the Law, and the Hand of God
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Now after this, in the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra the son of Seraiah, son of Azariah, son of Hilkiah,<sup>2</sup>son of Shallum, son of Zadok, son of Ahitub,<sup>3</sup>son of Amariah, son of Azariah, son of Meraioth,<sup>4</sup>son of Zerahiah, son of Uzzi, son of Bukki,<sup>5</sup>son of Abishua, son of Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the chief priest—<sup>6</sup>this Ezra went up from Babylonia. He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses that the LORD, the God of Israel, had given, and the king granted him all that he asked, for the hand of the LORD his God was on him.<sup>7</sup>And there went up also to Jerusalem, in the seventh year of Artaxerxes the king, some of the people of Israel, and some of the priests and Levites, the singers and gatekeepers, and the temple servants.<sup>8</sup>And Ezra came to Jerusalem in the fifth month, which was in the seventh year of the king.<sup>9</sup>For on the first day of the first month he began to go up from Babylonia, and on the first day of the fifth month he came to Jerusalem, for the good hand of his God was on him.<sup>10</sup>For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel.<sup>11</sup>This is a copy of the letter that King Artaxerxes gave to Ezra the priest, the scribe, a man learned in matters of the commandments of the LORD and his statutes for Israel:<sup>12</sup>"Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven. Peace. And now<sup>13</sup>I make a decree that anyone of the people of Israel or their priests or Levites in my kingdom, who freely offers to go to Jerusalem, may go with you.<sup>14</sup>For you are sent by the king and his seven counselors to make inquiries about Judah and Jerusalem according to the Law of your God, which is in your hand,<sup>15</sup>and also to carry the silver and gold that the king and his counselors have freely offered to the God of Israel, whose dwelling is in Jerusalem,<sup>16</sup>with all the silver and gold that you shall find in the whole province of Babylonia, and with the freewill offerings of the people and the priests, vowed willingly for the house of their God that is in Jerusalem.<sup>17</sup>With this money, then, you shall with all diligence buy bulls, rams, and lambs, with their grain offerings and their drink offerings, and you shall offer them on the altar of the house of your God that is in Jerusalem.<sup>18</sup>Whatever seems good to you and your brothers to do with the rest of the silver and gold, you may do, according to the will of your God.<sup>19</sup>The vessels that have been given you for the service of the house of your God, you shall deliver before the God of Jerusalem.<sup>20</sup>And whatever else is required for the house of your God, which it falls to you to provide, you may provide it out of the king's treasury.<sup>21</sup>"And I, Artaxerxes the king, make a decree to all the treasurers in the province Beyond the River: Whatever Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven, requires of you, let it be done with all diligence,<sup>22</sup>up to 100 talents of silver, 100 cors of wheat, 100 baths of wine, 100 baths of oil, and salt without prescribing how much.<sup>23</sup>Whatever is decreed by the God of heaven, let it be done in full for the house of the God of heaven, lest his wrath be against the realm of the king and his sons.<sup>24</sup>We also notify you that it shall not be lawful to impose tribute, custom, or toll on anyone of the priests, the Levites, the singers, the doorkeepers, the temple servants, or other servants of this house of God.<sup>25</sup>"And you, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God that is in your hand, appoint magistrates and judges who may judge all the people in the province Beyond the River, all such as know the laws of your God. And those who do not know them, you shall teach.<sup>26</sup>Whoever will not obey the law of your God and the law of the king, let judgment be strictly executed on him, whether for death or for banishment or for confiscation of his goods or for imprisonment."<sup>27</sup>Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king, to beautify the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem,<sup>28</sup>and who extended to me his steadfast love before the king and his counselors, and before all the king's mighty officers. I took courage, for the hand of the LORD my God was on me, and I gathered leading men from Israel to go up with me.
7.overview:
Fifty-eight years after the temple was finished, Ezra appears: a priest descended from Aaron through Zadok and through Hilkiah, who found the lost law in Josiah's day, and a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses. The king gives him everything he asks, for the hand of the LORD his God was on him (vv. 1-7). The journey takes four months, under the good hand of God, for Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel (vv. 8-10).

Artaxerxes' letter, given in its Aramaic, commissions him to examine Judah by the Law of your God, which is in your hand, to carry royal and freewill gold and silver for the altar, to draw on the treasury with salt unlimited, to exempt all the temple staff from tax, and to appoint judges and teach those who do not know God's laws (vv. 11-26). Then the text returns to Hebrew and to Ezra's own voice: Blessed be the LORD ... who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king, and who gave him courage by his hand to gather leaders for the journey (vv. 27-28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Hand of the LORD His God Was on Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now after this, in the reign of Artaxerxes, Ezra — his descent traced through Seraiah, Hilkiah and Zadok back to Aaron the chief priest (vv. 1-5) — goes up from Babylon. He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses that the LORD, the God of Israel, had given, and the king granted him all that he asked, for the hand of the LORD his God was on him (v. 6). A company of laymen, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants goes with him in Artaxerxes' seventh year (v. 7). They leave on the first day of the first month and arrive on the first day of the fifth, for the good hand of his God was on him (vv. 8-9). For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 10 explains verse 9 — it begins with for. The good hand of God was on Ezra, because Ezra had set his heart to study the law. And the order of the three verbs cannot be reversed: study first, then do, then teach. A man cannot teach honestly what he has not first obeyed, and he cannot obey what he has not first taken the trouble to know.
verseByVerse.examples: Ezra's genealogy runs through Hilkiah — the high priest who found the lost Book of the Law in a storeroom of Josiah's temple (2 Chr 34:14; 1 Chr 6:13-14). A century and a half later, the man who carries that book back to Jerusalem and teaches it to the nation is his descendant.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after this, in the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra the son of Seraiah, son of Azariah, son of Hilkiah, son of Shallum, son of Zadok, son of Ahitub, son of Amariah, son of Azariah, son of Meraioth, son of Zerahiah, son of Uzzi, son of Bukki, son of Abishua, son of Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the chief priest—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now after this, in the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra the son of Seraiah, son of Azariah, son of Hilkiah ...

Now after this. Three words, and fifty-eight years go by. The temple was finished in 516; Ezra arrives in 458. Everything in the book of Esther — Xerxes, the banquet, Haman, the decree, Mordecai at the gate — happens in the gap between the last verse of chapter 6 and the first verse of chapter 7. The house has been standing for two generations. The people who dedicated it are dead.

Then a genealogy, and it is not decoration. Ezra's line is traced back sixteen names to Aaron the chief priest, through Phinehas, whose zeal stopped a plague, and Zadok, David's faithful priest. It is selective — the full list in 1 Chronicles 6 has more generations — and son of here means descendant, because Seraiah, the first name, was the chief priest the Babylonians executed at Riblah in 586 (2 Kgs 25:18-21), a hundred and twenty-eight years before this journey. Seraiah's son Jehozadak went into exile (1 Chr 6:15), and his grandson was Jeshua, who built the altar in chapter 3.

And one name in the list should stop a reader who has just come through 2 Chronicles. Son of Hilkiah. First Chronicles puts Hilkiah two generations above Seraiah (1 Chr 6:13-14): he is the high priest of Josiah's reign — the man who, while the builders were carrying money out of a storeroom, found the Book of the Law of the LORD given through Moses (2 Chr 34:14).

The Bible had been lost in the house of God until Hilkiah found it. A century and a half later, the man who carries that same law back to Jerusalem and sets out to teach it to the whole nation is Hilkiah's descendant. Families carry more than blood. Somewhere in that line, through an exile and a burned temple, somebody kept telling the children about the book.

verseByVerse.quote: this Ezra went up from Babylonia. He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses that the LORD, the God of Israel, had given, and the king granted him all that he asked, for the hand of the LORD his God was on him. And there went up also to Jerusalem, in the seventh year of Artaxerxes the king, some of the people of Israel, and some of the priests and Levites, the singers and gatekeepers, and the temple servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This Ezra went up from Babylonia. He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses that the LORD, the God of Israel, had given.

A scribe skilled. The word for skilled is the one the psalmist uses of himself: my tongue is like the pen of a ready scribe (Ps 45:1). Quick, fluent, practised — a man for whom the law of Moses was not a reference work he looked things up in but the language he thought in. Ezra's priestly descent gave him his standing. His skill with the book gave him his usefulness.

And the king granted him all that he asked, for the hand of the LORD his God was on him.

There is the phrase that runs through the next two chapters. It will appear six times in chapters 7 and 8 — three times here, three times on the journey (7:6, 9, 28; 8:18, 22, 31) — and every time it is the explanation for something that should not have happened. Why did the most powerful king on earth give a Jewish scribe everything he asked for? Not because Ezra negotiated well. The hand of the LORD his God was on him.

And he did not go alone. There went up also to Jerusalem, in the seventh year of Artaxerxes the king, some of the people of Israel, and some of the priests and Levites, the singers and gatekeepers, and the temple servants. Every order of the temple community is represented again, as it was in chapter 2. A second return, smaller than the first, bringing the one thing the first had not brought with it in force: a teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: And Ezra came to Jerusalem in the fifth month, which was in the seventh year of the king. For on the first day of the first month he began to go up from Babylonia, and on the first day of the fifth month he came to Jerusalem, for the good hand of his God was on him. For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Ezra came to Jerusalem in the fifth month, which was in the seventh year of the king. For on the first day of the first month he began to go up from Babylonia, and on the first day of the fifth month he came to Jerusalem.

Four months, nine hundred miles, with families, animals and a great deal of gold. He began on the first day of the first month — the day, as it happens, on which Moses was told to set up the tabernacle and did (Exod 40:2, 17). Whether Ezra chose the date for that reason we are not told, but a scribe who knew the law as he did could hardly have missed it. (The caravan actually left the river Ahava on the twelfth, after a halt to gather Levites and to fast; 8:31 gives that date.)

For the good hand of his God was on him. Good, this time. Not only powerful but kind. The hand that could have crushed a small party on the desert roads kept it instead.

And then the verse this whole half of the book stands on.

For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel.

Notice first the little word at the front: for. Verse 10 gives the reason for verse 9. The good hand of God was on him because he had set his heart to study the law. God was not rewarding Ezra's diligence as though it earned something; but the man who had given his life to God's word is the man God's hand rested on, and the text wants us to see the two side by side.

Then the verbs. Set his heart and study — in Hebrew the very pair that runs through 2 Chronicles, where a man either set his heart to seek God or did not (2 Chr 12:14; 30:19). The word translated study is the word for seeking. What is new here is the object: Ezra set his heart to seek the law. He looked for God where God had spoken.

And the order: study it, do it, teach it. It will not run the other way round. A man cannot honestly teach what he has not first obeyed, and he cannot obey what he has not first taken the trouble to understand. Most failures in the ministry of the word are failures to keep that order — teaching without studying, which produces nonsense, or teaching without doing, which produces hypocrites.

This is not only a verse for preachers. Every parent teaches, every believer is watched by someone. The question verse 10 puts to all of us is simple: is the thing I pass on to others something I have first sat down with, and then lived in?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–26 — The Law of Your God, Which Is in Your Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king's letter to Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven (vv. 11-12): any Israelite who freely offers may go with him (v. 13); he is sent to inquire into Judah according to the Law of your God, which is in your hand (v. 14), carrying the king's gold and silver and the offerings of Babylon's Jews (vv. 15-16), to buy offerings for the altar (v. 17), use the rest as he and his brothers see fit (v. 18), deliver the vessels (v. 19) and draw on the treasury for anything else (v. 20). The provincial treasurers must supply him — silver, wheat, wine, oil, and salt without prescribing how much (vv. 21-22) — lest his wrath be against the realm of the king (v. 23); the temple staff are exempt from tax (v. 24). And Ezra is to appoint judges who know the law, and those who do not know them, you shall teach (vv. 25-26).
verseByVerse.theology: Two hands meet in this chapter. The hand of God is on Ezra (vv. 6, 9, 28), and the law of God is in Ezra's hand (v. 14) — which the king himself, in verse 25, calls the wisdom of your God that is in your hand. The man God holds is the man who holds God's word, and a Persian emperor could see the connection.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 25 writes teaching into imperial law. The king does not only authorise judges who already know God's statutes; he orders that those who do not know them be taught. Two centuries earlier Jehoshaphat sent Levites round the towns of Judah having the Book of the Law of the LORD with them (2 Chr 17:9). Now a pagan emperor sends a scribe to do it for a whole province.

verseByVerse.quote: This is a copy of the letter that King Artaxerxes gave to Ezra the priest, the scribe, a man learned in matters of the commandments of the LORD and his statutes for Israel: "Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven. Peace. And now I make a decree that anyone of the people of Israel or their priests or Levites in my kingdom, who freely offers to go to Jerusalem, may go with you. For you are sent by the king and his seven counselors to make inquiries about Judah and Jerusalem according to the Law of your God, which is in your hand, and also to carry the silver and gold that the king and his counselors have freely offered to the God of Israel, whose dwelling is in Jerusalem, with all the silver and gold that you shall find in the whole province of Babylonia, and with the freewill offerings of the people and the priests, vowed willingly for the house of their God that is in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the text gives us a copy of the king's letter, and from verse 12 to verse 26 it is in Aramaic, the language it was written in. The narrator introduces it with a third description of Ezra in six verses: Ezra the priest, the scribe, a man learned in matters of the commandments of the LORD and his statutes for Israel. A skilled scribe (v. 6), a man who had set his heart on the law (v. 10), a man learned in it (v. 11). The book will not let us forget what kind of man is being sent.

Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven. Peace.

King of kings was the Persian emperor's standard title. The man who styles himself king of kings is commissioning a scribe to teach the law of the one who actually is.

The first provision is a voluntary return: anyone of the people of Israel or their priests or Levites in my kingdom, who freely offers to go to Jerusalem, may go with you. Nobody is conscripted. As in chapter 1, the door is opened and people are left to walk through it.

Then Ezra's brief. For you are sent by the king and his seven counselors to make inquiries about Judah and Jerusalem according to the Law of your God, which is in your hand.

Which is in your hand. Keep that phrase next to the one in verse 6. The hand of the LORD was on Ezra; the law of the LORD was in Ezra's hand. God held the man who held God's word. The king saw the scroll he carried and understood that it was the standard by which Jerusalem was to be examined — not the king's own laws, and not the customs of the province.

And notice who is sending him: the king and his seven counselors. The book of Esther names that council — the seven princes of Persia and Media, who saw the king's face, and sat first in the kingdom (Esth 1:14) — and it was their advice, in the reign of this king's father, that had Queen Vashti deposed by a decree of the Medes and Persians. A generation later the same body of men is voting gold for the God of Israel.

And he is to carry silver and gold: the silver and gold that the king and his counselors have freely offered to the God of Israel, whose dwelling is in Jerusalem, with whatever the province of Babylon will give, and the freewill offerings of the people and the priests. A Persian king and his cabinet giving freewill offerings to the God of Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: With this money, then, you shall with all diligence buy bulls, rams, and lambs, with their grain offerings and their drink offerings, and you shall offer them on the altar of the house of your God that is in Jerusalem. Whatever seems good to you and your brothers to do with the rest of the silver and gold, you may do, according to the will of your God. The vessels that have been given you for the service of the house of your God, you shall deliver before the God of Jerusalem. And whatever else is required for the house of your God, which it falls to you to provide, you may provide it out of the king's treasury.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With this money, then, you shall with all diligence buy bulls, rams, and lambs, with their grain offerings and their drink offerings, and you shall offer them on the altar of the house of your God that is in Jerusalem.

The first use of the money is the altar. Before salaries, before buildings, before anything else: offerings. The king seems to have understood what the house was for.

And then an extraordinary grant of trust. Whatever seems good to you and your brothers to do with the rest of the silver and gold, you may do, according to the will of your God. No accounting to the treasury, no schedule of approved expenditure. Ezra and his colleagues are to decide, and the standard for deciding is the will of their God. The king was willing to be governed, at one remove, by a law he had never read.

The vessels given for the house are to be delivered before the God of Jerusalem, and anything further that the house requires, Ezra may draw from the royal treasury. It is Darius's decree of chapter 6 renewed and enlarged by his grandson.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I, Artaxerxes the king, make a decree to all the treasurers in the province Beyond the River: Whatever Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven, requires of you, let it be done with all diligence, up to 100 talents of silver, 100 cors of wheat, 100 baths of wine, 100 baths of oil, and salt without prescribing how much. Whatever is decreed by the God of heaven, let it be done in full for the house of the God of heaven, lest his wrath be against the realm of the king and his sons. We also notify you that it shall not be lawful to impose tribute, custom, or toll on anyone of the priests, the Levites, the singers, the doorkeepers, the temple servants, or other servants of this house of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second part of the letter is addressed to the provincial treasurers, and it reads like a blank cheque with a ceiling. Whatever Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven, requires of you, let it be done with all diligence, up to 100 talents of silver, 100 cors of wheat, 100 baths of wine, 100 baths of oil, and salt without prescribing how much.

Salt without limit. The law required that every grain offering be seasoned with salt, the salt of the covenant with your God (Lev 2:13), and the king's clerks, whether they knew it or not, wrote no ceiling on it.

Then the king's motive, and it is frank. Whatever is decreed by the God of heaven, let it be done in full for the house of the God of heaven, lest his wrath be against the realm of the king and his sons. Artaxerxes is afraid of Israel's God. He does not worship him, but he does not want to be on the wrong side of him, and he is prepared to pay to stay on the right side. It is not faith. It is, however, more sense than many people have.

And the tax exemption: no tribute, custom or toll on any priest, Levite, singer, doorkeeper, temple servant or other servant of the house. The words are the same three that the accusers of chapter 4 used to frighten this king's predecessors — tribute, custom, toll (4:13). They are now written down as the things the servants of the house will never have to pay.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God that is in your hand, appoint magistrates and judges who may judge all the people in the province Beyond the River, all such as know the laws of your God. And those who do not know them, you shall teach. Whoever will not obey the law of your God and the law of the king, let judgment be strictly executed on him, whether for death or for banishment or for confiscation of his goods or for imprisonment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God that is in your hand, appoint magistrates and judges who may judge all the people in the province Beyond the River, all such as know the laws of your God. And those who do not know them, you shall teach.

The wisdom of your God that is in your hand. In verse 14 the king called it the law of your God; here he calls it the wisdom of your God, and he means the same scroll. A Persian emperor has put it better than many theologians: the law of God is not an arbitrary list of restrictions but his wisdom, written down, and it can be carried in one man's hand.

Two tasks. Appoint judges from among those who already know God's statutes. And those who do not know them, you shall teach. The Persian crown has written teaching into law. Two hundred years earlier Jehoshaphat sent Levites round Judah having the Book of the Law of the LORD with them (2 Chr 17:9); now an emperor sends a scribe to do the same for a province that stretches from the Euphrates to Egypt.

Verse 26 attaches penalties to disobedience — death, banishment, confiscation, prison — for anyone who will not obey the law of your God and the law of the king. That is Persian civil enforcement, and it belongs to a particular moment when a community's religious law was also its civil law under an imperial governor. It is not a pattern for the church, whose Lord gave it no sword and whose weapons, Paul says, are not of the flesh (2 Cor 10:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–28 — Blessed Be the LORD, the God of Our Fathers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezra breaks into blessing, in his own voice: Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king, to beautify the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem (v. 27), and who extended to me his steadfast love before the king and his counselors ... I took courage, for the hand of the LORD my God was on me, and I gathered leading men from Israel to go up with me (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: The letter was written by a king, the treasury was the king's, and the first thing Ezra does with it is give the credit away. God put the thing into the king's heart. God showed him steadfast love in front of the court. God's hand gave him courage. There is not a word here about his own qualifications, and chapter 7 has just spent five verses listing them.
verseByVerse.examples: At verse 27 the text changes language and voice at once. The king's letter was in Aramaic; Ezra's blessing is in Hebrew, and in the first person. From here to the end of chapter 9 the book is Ezra's own account, in his own words.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king, to beautify the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem, and who extended to me his steadfast love before the king and his counselors, and before all the king's mighty officers. I took courage, for the hand of the LORD my God was on me, and I gathered leading men from Israel to go up with me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king, to beautify the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem.

Suddenly the voice changes. The king's letter was in Aramaic; this is Hebrew. The narrator has been speaking about Ezra; now Ezra speaks, in the first person, and he stays in the first person to the end of chapter 9. The first words of his own account are a blessing.

And the first thing he blesses God for is the king's heart. He has just been handed the most generous commission in the book, drafted by a Persian chancery and sealed by the king of kings, and he does not admire the king for it. Who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king. The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD (Prov 21:1), and Ezra knows whose hand turned it.

And who extended to me his steadfast love before the king and his counselors, and before all the king's mighty officers.
