Steadfast love — chesed, the covenant love the singers sang over the foundation in chapter 3 — shown to one man in a room full of Persian officials. God's faithfulness to his people did not stop at the border of the promised land.

I took courage, for the hand of the LORD my God was on me, and I gathered leading men from Israel to go up with me.

I took courage — the word for a man bracing himself, used of Jehoiada before his coup (2 Chr 23:1). Ezra did not feel brave because the letter was generous. He took courage because of whose hand was on him, and then he did the next practical thing, which was to gather people.

The scribe who set his heart to study the law and do it and teach it was a gift to his generation, and he was a shadow of someone greater. There came a Teacher who did not need to study the law to learn it, because he had given it; who did it perfectly; and who, on the road to Emmaus, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets ... interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself, and then opened their minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:27, 45). Ezra carried the book in his hand. The book is about him.

7.theology:
Verse 10 is the heart of the second half of Ezra, and it begins with for: the good hand of God rested on the man who had set his heart to seek the law. The order of its verbs is fixed — study, do, teach — and every ministry of the word stands or falls by keeping it.

Two hands meet in the chapter. God's hand is on Ezra (vv. 6, 9, 28); God's law is in Ezra's hand (v. 14), which the king himself calls the wisdom of your God (v. 25). And every open door is credited upward: the king's generosity was God putting it into his heart (v. 27). The man who holds God's word is the man God holds, and he gives the credit away.
7.examples:
The whole story of Esther happens between the last verse of chapter 6 and the first verse of chapter 7.

Ezra was descended from Hilkiah, who found the Book of the Law lost in a temple storeroom; his descendant carried it back to Jerusalem.

The hand of God is named six times in chapters 7 and 8, every time explaining something that should not have happened.

He left Babylon on the first day of the first month, the day the tabernacle was first set up.

A Persian king called the law of Moses the wisdom of your God, and wrote into his decree that those who did not know it must be taught.

The king wrote no limit on the salt.

The first words of Ezra's own account are a blessing, and they give the credit for the king's generosity to God.

8.title: The Journey of Faith: Fasting, Prayer, and the Treasure Carried to Jerusalem
8.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the heads of their fathers' houses, and this is the genealogy of those who went up with me from Babylonia, in the reign of Artaxerxes the king:<sup>2</sup>Of the sons of Phinehas, Gershom. Of the sons of Ithamar, Daniel. Of the sons of David, Hattush.<sup>3</sup>Of the sons of Shecaniah, who was of the sons of Parosh, Zechariah, with whom were registered 150 men.<sup>4</sup>Of the sons of Pahath-moab, Eliehoenai the son of Zerahiah, and with him 200 men.<sup>5</sup>Of the sons of Zattu, Shecaniah the son of Jahaziel, and with him 300 men.<sup>6</sup>Of the sons of Adin, Ebed the son of Jonathan, and with him 50 men.<sup>7</sup>Of the sons of Elam, Jeshaiah the son of Athaliah, and with him 70 men.<sup>8</sup>Of the sons of Shephatiah, Zebadiah the son of Michael, and with him 80 men.<sup>9</sup>Of the sons of Joab, Obadiah the son of Jehiel, and with him 218 men.<sup>10</sup>Of the sons of Bani, Shelomith the son of Josiphiah, and with him 160 men.<sup>11</sup>Of the sons of Bebai, Zechariah, the son of Bebai, and with him 28 men.<sup>12</sup>Of the sons of Azgad, Johanan the son of Hakkatan, and with him 110 men.<sup>13</sup>Of the sons of Adonikam, those who came later, their names being Eliphelet, Jeuel, and Shemaiah, and with them 60 men.<sup>14</sup>Of the sons of Bigvai, Uthai and Zaccur, and with them 70 men.<sup>15</sup>I gathered them to the river that runs to Ahava, and there we camped three days. As I reviewed the people and the priests, I found there none of the sons of Levi.<sup>16</sup>Then I sent for Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, and Meshullam, leading men, and for Joiarib and Elnathan, who were men of insight,<sup>17</sup>and sent them to Iddo, the leading man at the place Casiphia, telling them what to say to Iddo and his brothers and the temple servants at the place Casiphia, namely, to send us ministers for the house of our God.<sup>18</sup>And by the good hand of our God on us, they brought us a man of discretion, of the sons of Mahli the son of Levi, son of Israel, namely Sherebiah with his sons and kinsmen, 18;<sup>19</sup>also Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, with his kinsmen and their sons, 20;<sup>20</sup>besides 220 of the temple servants, whom David and his officials had set apart to attend the Levites. These were all mentioned by name.<sup>21</sup>Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river Ahava, that we might humble ourselves before our God, to seek from him a safe journey for ourselves, our children, and all our goods.<sup>22</sup>For I was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers and horsemen to protect us against the enemy on our way, since we had told the king, "The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him, and the power of his wrath is against all who forsake him."<sup>23</sup>So we fasted and implored our God for this, and he listened to our entreaty.<sup>24</sup>Then I set apart twelve of the leading priests: Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their kinsmen with them.<sup>25</sup>And I weighed out to them the silver and the gold and the vessels, the offering for the house of our God that the king and his counselors and his lords and all Israel there present had offered.<sup>26</sup>I weighed out into their hand 650 talents of silver, and silver vessels worth 200 talents, and 100 talents of gold,<sup>27</sup>20 bowls of gold worth 1,000 darics, and two vessels of fine bright bronze as precious as gold.<sup>28</sup>And I said to them, "You are holy to the LORD, and the vessels are holy, and the silver and the gold are a freewill offering to the LORD, the God of your fathers.<sup>29</sup>Guard them and keep them until you weigh them before the chief priests and the Levites and the heads of fathers' houses in Israel at Jerusalem, within the chambers of the house of the LORD."<sup>30</sup>So the priests and the Levites took over the weight of the silver and the gold and the vessels, to bring them to Jerusalem, to the house of our God.<sup>31</sup>Then we departed from the river Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, to go to Jerusalem. The hand of our God was on us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy and from ambushes by the way.<sup>32</sup>We came to Jerusalem, and there we remained three days.<sup>33</sup>On the fourth day, within the house of our God, the silver and the gold and the vessels were weighed into the hands of Meremoth the priest, son of Uriah, and with him was Eleazar the son of Phinehas, and with them were the Levites, Jozabad the son of Jeshua and Noadiah the son of Binnui.<sup>34</sup>The whole was counted and weighed, and the weight of everything was recorded.<sup>35</sup>At that time those who had come from captivity, the returned exiles, offered burnt offerings to the God of Israel, twelve bulls for all Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and as a sin offering twelve male goats. All this was a burnt offering to the LORD.<sup>36</sup>They also delivered the king's commissions to the king's satraps and to the governors of the province Beyond the River, and they aided the people and the house of God.
8.overview: Ezra lists those who travelled with him — priests, a son of David, and twelve lay families, 1,496 men — and at the Ahava canal finds that not one of them is a Levite. He sends a scripted delegation to Casiphia and, by the good hand of our God, thirty-eight Levites and 220 temple servants come (vv. 1-20). He proclaims a fast, ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers, because he had told the king that God's hand is for good on all who seek him and against all who forsake him — and God listened (vv. 21-23). He weighs out a fortune in silver and gold to priests and Levites — you are holy to the LORD, and the vessels are holy — to be guarded until it is weighed in Jerusalem (vv. 24-30). God delivers the caravan from the enemy and from ambushes; in Jerusalem the whole is weighed, and the weight of everything was recorded; offerings are made for all Israel and the king's orders delivered (vv. 31-36).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — I Found There None of the Sons of Levi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezra lists those who went with him: two priestly families, of the sons of David, Hattush (vv. 1-2), and twelve lay families with their men, fifteen hundred in all (vv. 3-14). He gathers them at the river that runs to Ahava, camps three days, reviews them — and I found there none of the sons of Levi (v. 15). So he sends eleven leading men, with their message scripted, to Iddo at Casiphia to ask for ministers for the house (vv. 16-17), and by the good hand of our God on us they bring back Sherebiah, a man of discretion, and Hashabiah, thirty-eight Levites in all, with 220 temple servants, all mentioned by name (vv. 18-20).
verseByVerse.theology: The problem of 2:40 has not gone away in eighty years: the first return brought seventy-four Levites, and this one, at first, brought none. The men whose work was the hard daily service of the house would not leave Babylon for it. Ezra did not set off without them and hope. He stopped the caravan for three days and went and asked.
verseByVerse.examples: Sherebiah was a last-minute recruit, fetched from a settlement by the canal because the caravan was short of Levites. Years later, when Ezra stood on a wooden platform in Jerusalem and read the law to the whole people, Sherebiah was one of the Levites who helped the people to understand the Law (Neh 8:7). The man who was found almost by accident became one of the book's teachers.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the heads of their fathers' houses, and this is the genealogy of those who went up with me from Babylonia, in the reign of Artaxerxes the king: Of the sons of Phinehas, Gershom. Of the sons of Ithamar, Daniel. Of the sons of David, Hattush. Of the sons of Shecaniah, who was of the sons of Parosh, Zechariah, with whom were registered 150 men. Of the sons of Pahath-moab, Eliehoenai the son of Zerahiah, and with him 200 men. Of the sons of Zattu, Shecaniah the son of Jahaziel, and with him 300 men. Of the sons of Adin, Ebed the son of Jonathan, and with him 50 men. Of the sons of Elam, Jeshaiah the son of Athaliah, and with him 70 men. Of the sons of Shephatiah, Zebadiah the son of Michael, and with him 80 men. Of the sons of Joab, Obadiah the son of Jehiel, and with him 218 men. Of the sons of Bani, Shelomith the son of Josiphiah, and with him 160 men. Of the sons of Bebai, Zechariah, the son of Bebai, and with him 28 men. Of the sons of Azgad, Johanan the son of Hakkatan, and with him 110 men. Of the sons of Adonikam, those who came later, their names being Eliphelet, Jeuel, and Shemaiah, and with them 60 men. Of the sons of Bigvai, Uthai and Zaccur, and with them 70 men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are the heads of their fathers' houses, and this is the genealogy of those who went up with me from Babylonia, in the reign of Artaxerxes the king.

With me. Ezra's own account continues, and the list is his: the people he travelled with, whose names he knew.

First the priests — Gershom of the line of Phinehas, Daniel of the line of Ithamar — and then a name that matters: Of the sons of David, Hattush. First Chronicles traces Hattush several generations down from Zerubbabel (1 Chr 3:19-22). The house of David has no throne and no kingdom, but it has a member walking in this caravan, and somebody still knew exactly whose descendant he was.

Then twelve lay families, each with its head named and its men counted: a hundred and fifty of the sons of Parosh, two hundred of Pahath-moab, three hundred of Zattu, down to twenty-eight of the sons of Bebai. Add them and they come to 1,496 men, with their wives and children besides — a small company beside the forty-two thousand of chapter 2.

And almost every family name on this list is a family name from that list. The sons of Parosh, of Pahath-moab, of Zattu, of Adin, of Elam: their cousins went home with Zerubbabel eighty years before. These are the branches that stayed behind, and now, a generation or two later, they are following. Some families take two journeys to get home.

The text says so itself at verse 13. Of the sons of Adonikam, those who came later. Six hundred and sixty-six of Adonikam's family went home with Zerubbabel (2:13). The rest of them — Eliphelet, Jeuel, Shemaiah and sixty men — are described exactly as what they were: the ones who came later. God's timetable for a family is not always the same for every member of it.

verseByVerse.quote: I gathered them to the river that runs to Ahava, and there we camped three days. As I reviewed the people and the priests, I found there none of the sons of Levi. Then I sent for Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, and Meshullam, leading men, and for Joiarib and Elnathan, who were men of insight, and sent them to Iddo, the leading man at the place Casiphia, telling them what to say to Iddo and his brothers and the temple servants at the place Casiphia, namely, to send us ministers for the house of our God. And by the good hand of our God on us, they brought us a man of discretion, of the sons of Mahli the son of Levi, son of Israel, namely Sherebiah with his sons and kinsmen, 18; also Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, with his kinsmen and their sons, 20; besides 220 of the temple servants, whom David and his officials had set apart to attend the Levites. These were all mentioned by name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I gathered them to the river that runs to Ahava, and there we camped three days. As I reviewed the people and the priests, I found there none of the sons of Levi.

None. Not a single Levite in the caravan. It is the problem of chapter 2 in a sharper form: the first return had brought seventy-four Levites to more than four thousand priests (2:40), and this one had brought nobody at all. The men whose work was the carrying, the cleaning, the slaughtering, the teaching — the daily, heavy, unglamorous service of the house — had settled in Babylon and were not coming.

Ezra could have gone without them. He stopped instead. Then I sent for Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, and Meshullam, leading men, and for Joiarib and Elnathan, who were men of insight — eleven envoys, three of them called Elnathan, which says something about the popular names of that generation — and sent them to Iddo, the leading man at the place Casiphia, telling them what to say.

Telling them what to say. He scripted the approach. A request for ministers is too important to leave to improvisation.

And by the good hand of our God on us, they brought us a man of discretion, of the sons of Mahli the son of Levi, son of Israel, namely Sherebiah with his sons and kinsmen, 18; also Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, with his kinsmen and their sons, 20. Thirty-eight Levites, and two hundred and twenty temple servants besides, all mentioned by name.

Remember the name Sherebiah. Years later, when Ezra read the law aloud to the whole city from a wooden platform, a group of Levites went among the crowd and helped the people to understand the Law, reading clearly and giving the sense (Neh 8:7-8). Sherebiah is on that list. The man fetched at the last minute because the caravan was short of Levites spent his life explaining the book.

The temple servants came too, whom David and his officials had set apart to attend the Levites — an order of service that went back five hundred years to David's organising of the house, still recognised and still answering when called.

And Ezra does not credit his own recruiting. By the good hand of our God on us. The people who join a work of God are also his gift.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–23 — I Was Ashamed to Ask the King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river Ahava, that we might humble ourselves before our God, to seek from him a safe journey for ourselves, our children, and all our goods (v. 21). For I was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers and horsemen to protect us against the enemy on our way, since we had told the king, The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him, and the power of his wrath is against all who forsake him (v. 22). So we fasted and implored our God for this, and he listened to our entreaty (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: What Ezra told the king is 2 Chronicles in one sentence. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you (2 Chr 15:2): seek and forsake, the two great verbs of that book, and Ezra had said them to a Persian emperor. Having said them, he had to travel as though they were true.
verseByVerse.examples: Ezra is honest enough to write that he was ashamed — not of trusting God, but of being seen to contradict himself. Nehemiah, years later, accepted an armed escort from the same king (Neh 2:9), and the Bible does not rebuke either man. Ezra had put his words on record before the court, and the fast was what integrity looked like once the words had been said.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river Ahava, that we might humble ourselves before our God, to seek from him a safe journey for ourselves, our children, and all our goods. For I was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers and horsemen to protect us against the enemy on our way, since we had told the king, "The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him, and the power of his wrath is against all who forsake him." So we fasted and implored our God for this, and he listened to our entreaty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river Ahava, that we might humble ourselves before our God, to seek from him a safe journey for ourselves, our children, and all our goods.

Humble ourselves, and seek — the shape of the promise God gave at the dedication of the first temple, if my people ... humble themselves, and pray and seek my face (2 Chr 7:14). They had a nine-hundred-mile road ahead, children, and a fortune in gold. They went on their faces by the canal.

And then Ezra writes one of the most honest sentences in the Old Testament.

For I was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers and horsemen to protect us against the enemy on our way, since we had told the king, The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him, and the power of his wrath is against all who forsake him.

He was ashamed. Not ashamed of God, and not above asking for help. He had stood in front of the Persian court and said, in effect, that his God protects those who seek him and opposes those who forsake him. To go back a few weeks later and ask for cavalry would have told the king what Ezra actually believed.

Look at what he had told the king. Seek and forsake: those are the two great verbs of 2 Chronicles, joined in one sentence by the prophet Azariah — if you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you (2 Chr 15:2). Ezra had preached the theology of that whole book to a pagan emperor. Now he had to travel as though it were true.

That is a kind of faith most believers know something about: the faith that has said something out loud, in front of people who are watching, and now has to live up to it. The words were easy at court. They were harder at the edge of the desert with the children loaded on the donkeys.

This is not a rule that faith refuses soldiers. Nehemiah, sent by the same king a few years later, travelled with officers of the army and horsemen (Neh 2:9), and nobody rebukes him. Ezra's case was particular: he had said a particular thing, and integrity required him to stand on it. So he did what faithful people do with the fear that remains after they have made their decision. He took it to God.

So we fasted and implored our God for this, and he listened to our entreaty. It is the word used when God was moved by the prayer of Manasseh in chains (2 Chr 33:13). The God who let himself be entreated by the worst king in Judah let himself be entreated by a frightened scribe beside a canal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–36 — The Weight of Everything Was Recorded
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezra sets apart twelve leading priests, with the Levites Sherebiah and Hashabiah and their kinsmen (v. 24), and weighs out to them the offering — about six hundred and fifty talents of silver, silver vessels, a hundred talents of gold, gold bowls and two vessels of fine bronze (vv. 25-27). You are holy to the LORD, and the vessels are holy; guard them and keep them until you weigh them in Jerusalem (vv. 28-30). They leave Ahava on the twelfth of the first month, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy and from ambushes by the way (v. 31). Three days' rest in Jerusalem (v. 32); on the fourth, everything is weighed into the hands of the priests, and the weight of everything was recorded (vv. 33-34). They offer burnt offerings and a sin offering for all Israel (v. 35), and deliver the king's orders to the governors (v. 36).
verseByVerse.theology: Holy people carrying holy things. Ezra told the treasurers that they were holy to the LORD as well as the vessels — both set apart, both belonging to God — and then he gave them a very practical instruction: guard it, and have it weighed at the other end. Holiness and accountability are not rivals. The more sacred the trust, the more carefully it is counted.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 31 does not say there were no enemies. It says God delivered us from the hand of the enemy and from ambushes by the way. There were ambushes on the road. The prayer at Ahava was not answered by an empty desert; it was answered by a God whose hand was stronger than the hands that lay in wait.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I set apart twelve of the leading priests: Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their kinsmen with them. And I weighed out to them the silver and the gold and the vessels, the offering for the house of our God that the king and his counselors and his lords and all Israel there present had offered. I weighed out into their hand 650 talents of silver, and silver vessels worth 200 talents, and 100 talents of gold, 20 bowls of gold worth 1,000 darics, and two vessels of fine bright bronze as precious as gold. And I said to them, "You are holy to the LORD, and the vessels are holy, and the silver and the gold are a freewill offering to the LORD, the God of your fathers. Guard them and keep them until you weigh them before the chief priests and the Levites and the heads of fathers' houses in Israel at Jerusalem, within the chambers of the house of the LORD." So the priests and the Levites took over the weight of the silver and the gold and the vessels, to bring them to Jerusalem, to the house of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I set apart twelve of the leading priests: Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their kinsmen with them.

A careful reader will stop here, because Sherebiah and Hashabiah were introduced six verses ago as Levites, not priests. And verse 30 says it was the priests and the Levites who took charge of the treasure. The likeliest sense is that Ezra appointed twelve leading priests and, alongside them, these two Levites with ten of their kinsmen — priests and Levites sharing the charge. The Hebrew allows it, and the rest of the passage requires it.

Then he weighed the treasure out to them, and the figures are enormous: six hundred and fifty talents of silver — something over twenty tonnes — silver vessels worth two hundred talents, a hundred talents of gold, twenty gold bowls worth a thousand darics, and two vessels of fine bright bronze as precious as gold. All of it to be carried nine hundred miles without an escort.

And I said to them, You are holy to the LORD, and the vessels are holy, and the silver and the gold are a freewill offering to the LORD, the God of your fathers.

You are holy, and the vessels are holy. The men and the metal both set apart, both belonging to God. They were not couriers who happened to be carrying religious property. They were holy men entrusted with holy things.

And then the most practical sentence imaginable. Guard them and keep them until you weigh them before the chief priests and the Levites and the heads of fathers' houses in Israel at Jerusalem. Weighed out at Ahava; weighed in at Jerusalem. The holiness of the trust did not make the accounting unnecessary. It made it essential.

Anyone who handles what belongs to God — money given for his work, the care of his people, the teaching of his word — should hear both halves of that. You are holy to the LORD, and it will be weighed at the other end.

verseByVerse.quote: Then we departed from the river Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, to go to Jerusalem. The hand of our God was on us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy and from ambushes by the way. We came to Jerusalem, and there we remained three days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then we departed from the river Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, to go to Jerusalem. The hand of our God was on us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy and from ambushes by the way.

Four months of road in one sentence, and the sentence is honest. It does not say there were no enemies. It says God delivered them from the hand of the enemy and from ambushes by the way. There were people waiting for a caravan carrying twenty tonnes of silver, and they waited in vain.

The prayer at Ahava was not answered by an empty desert. It was answered by a stronger hand. Two hands are in the verse: the hand of our God on us, and the hand of the enemy against us, and the first held.

That is usually how God answers the prayer for protection. Not by removing every threat from the road, but by bringing his people through the threats. A believer who expects the first will be disillusioned; a believer who expects the second will find it true.

That hand is now counted six times in two chapters — on Ezra before the king, on him for the road, on him when he took courage, on the caravan when the Levites came, the hand for good on all who seek him, and the hand on the road (7:6, 9, 28; 8:18, 22, 31).

We came to Jerusalem, and there we remained three days. After four months, three days to rest before anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: On the fourth day, within the house of our God, the silver and the gold and the vessels were weighed into the hands of Meremoth the priest, son of Uriah, and with him was Eleazar the son of Phinehas, and with them were the Levites, Jozabad the son of Jeshua and Noadiah the son of Binnui. The whole was counted and weighed, and the weight of everything was recorded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the fourth day, within the house of our God, the silver and the gold and the vessels were weighed into the hands of Meremoth the priest, son of Uriah, and with him was Eleazar the son of Phinehas, and with them were the Levites, Jozabad the son of Jeshua and Noadiah the son of Binnui.

Four named men received it, two priests and two Levites — the same balance of offices that carried it.

And the first name is one to linger over. Nehemiah gives this man's full descent: Meremoth the son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz (Neh 3:4). Hakkoz. Turn back to chapter 2. When the first returnees arrived eighty years earlier, three priestly families sought their registration among those enrolled in the genealogies, but they were not found there, and were barred from the priesthood until a priest could consult Urim and Thummim — and one of those three was the sons of Hakkoz (2:61-63).

Now a son of Hakkoz is called Meremoth the priest, standing in the house of God with the treasure weighed into his hands. The text does not tell us how the question was settled. It simply shows us the family that could not find its name in the register, two generations later, entrusted with the gold of the house. The door that was shut until had opened.

The whole was counted and weighed, and the weight of everything was recorded.

The weight of everything. Twenty tonnes of silver, three tonnes of gold, the bowls, the bronze, carried nine hundred miles past ambushes, and it came out right on the scales in the house of God. Nothing was missing, and the fact was written down.

Paul would write that he took pains with the collection he was carrying to Jerusalem so that no one should blame us about this generous gift (2 Cor 8:20). Ezra had the same instinct four and a half centuries earlier. The honour of God was bound up with the honesty of the men carrying his gold.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time those who had come from captivity, the returned exiles, offered burnt offerings to the God of Israel, twelve bulls for all Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and as a sin offering twelve male goats. All this was a burnt offering to the LORD. They also delivered the king's commissions to the king's satraps and to the governors of the province Beyond the River, and they aided the people and the house of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that time those who had come from captivity, the returned exiles, offered burnt offerings to the God of Israel, twelve bulls for all Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and as a sin offering twelve male goats.

Twelve bulls and twelve goats for all Israel, and ninety-six rams — eight for each tribe. Like the returnees of chapter 6, this company offers for every tribe, though it came from only a few. They would not let Israel shrink to the size of whoever had made the journey.

They also delivered the king's commissions to the king's satraps and to the governors of the province Beyond the River, and they aided the people and the house of God. The king's letter of chapter 7 is handed to the officials, and they do what it says.

The chapter has two words that belong together. At Ahava, Ezra was ashamed to ask the king for protection, because he had said God would guard those who seek him. And he told the priests to guard the treasure until it was weighed in Jerusalem. Five centuries later, writing from a prison with his own life nearly spent, the apostle put both words in one sentence: But I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me (2 Tim 1:12). Ezra's gold came out right on the scales because a hand was on the caravan. Everything a believer has entrusted to Christ will come out right on the last day for the same reason: no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28).

8.theology:
Ezra's words to the king in verse 22 are the two great verbs of 2 Chronicles — seek and forsake (2 Chr 15:2) — said to a pagan emperor, and the fast at Ahava is what integrity looks like once such words have been said in public. The prayer was answered not by an empty road but by deliverance from ambushes by the way (v. 31): God's protection runs through danger, not around it.

Verses 24-34 bind holiness to accountability. The men and the gold are both holy to the LORD, and both are weighed at the other end. The more sacred a trust, the more carefully it is counted — and Paul's words about the deposit Christ guards until that day (2 Tim 1:12) are this chapter's shape carried into the gospel.
8.examples:
There was not one Levite in the caravan, so Ezra stopped for three days and sent to ask.

Three of the eleven men he sent were called Elnathan.

Sherebiah, recruited at the last minute, later helped the whole city understand the law when it was read (Neh 8:7).

Ezra wrote that he was ashamed to ask for soldiers after telling the king his God protected those who seek him.

Nehemiah later took an armed escort from the same king, and the Bible rebukes neither man.

There were ambushes on the road, and the caravan came through them.

Twenty tonnes of silver travelled nine hundred miles and came out right on the scales in the house of God.

9.title: Ezra's Great Prayer: Intercessory Identification and the Gravity of Sin
9.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things had been done, the officials approached me and said, "The people of Israel and the priests and the Levites have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands with their abominations, from the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians, and the Amorites.<sup>2</sup>For they have taken some of their daughters to be wives for themselves and for their sons, so that the holy race has mixed itself with the peoples of the lands. And in this faithlessness the hand of the officials and chief men has been foremost."<sup>3</sup>As soon as I heard this, I tore my garment and my cloak and pulled hair from my head and beard and sat appalled.<sup>4</sup>Then all who trembled at the words of the God of Israel, because of the faithlessness of the returned exiles, gathered around me while I sat appalled until the evening sacrifice.<sup>5</sup>And at the evening sacrifice I rose from my fasting, with my garment and my cloak torn, and fell upon my knees and spread out my hands to the LORD my God,<sup>6</sup>saying: "O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you, my God, for our iniquities have risen higher than our heads, and our guilt has mounted up to the heavens.<sup>7</sup>From the days of our fathers to this day we have been in great guilt. And for our iniquities we, our kings, and our priests have been given into the hand of the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, to plundering, and to utter shame, as it is today.<sup>8</sup>But now for a brief moment favor has been shown by the LORD our God, to leave us a remnant and to give us a secure hold within his holy place, that our God may brighten our eyes and grant us a little reviving in our slavery.<sup>9</sup>For we are slaves. Yet our God has not forsaken us in our slavery, but has extended to us his steadfast love before the kings of Persia, to grant us some reviving to set up the house of our God, to repair its ruins, and to give us protection in Judea and Jerusalem.<sup>10</sup>"And now, O our God, what shall we say after this? For we have forsaken your commandments,<sup>11</sup>which you commanded by your servants the prophets, saying, 'The land that you are entering, to take possession of it, is a land impure with the impurity of the peoples of the lands, with their abominations that have filled it from end to end with their uncleanness.<sup>12</sup>Therefore do not give your daughters to their sons, neither take their daughters for your sons, and never seek their peace or prosperity, that you may be strong and eat the good of the land and leave it for an inheritance to your children forever.'<sup>13</sup>And after all that has come upon us for our evil deeds and for our great guilt, seeing that you, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserved and have given us such a remnant as this,<sup>14</sup>shall we break your commandments again and intermarry with the peoples who practice these abominations? Would you not be angry with us until you consumed us, so that there should be no remnant, nor any to escape?<sup>15</sup>O LORD, the God of Israel, you are just, for we are left a remnant that has escaped, as it is today. Behold, we are before you in our guilt, for none can stand before you because of this."
9.overview: Officials report to Ezra that the people, priests and Levites — with the leaders foremost — have married into the households of the peoples of the land, named in the law's own list, so that the holy race has mixed itself with them (vv. 1-2). The issue is worship, not blood: the law forbade such marriages because they would turn away your sons from following me (Deut 7:4), and Ruth the Moabite, who took Israel's God as hers, is David's great-grandmother. Ezra tears his clothes, pulls out his own hair, and sits appalled till the evening sacrifice, surrounded by those who tremble at God's words (vv. 3-4). Then, kneeling with hands spread as Solomon did (v. 5), he prays: ashamed, confessing our iniquities from the fathers to this day (vv. 6-7), thanking God for a brief reviving — our God has not forsaken us (vv. 8-9) — confessing we have forsaken your commandments (vv. 10-12), and ending with no request at all: you are just ... none can stand before you (vv. 13-15).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The officials come to Ezra: the people, the priests and the Levites have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands with their abominations (v. 1), for they have taken some of their daughters to be wives for themselves and for their sons, so that the holy race has mixed itself with the peoples of the lands. And in this faithlessness the hand of the officials and chief men has been foremost (v. 2). Ezra tears his garment and cloak, pulls hair from his head and beard, and sits appalled (v. 3); all who trembled at the words of the God of Israel gather round him until the evening sacrifice (v. 4). Then he rises, falls on his knees and spreads out his hands to the LORD his God (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The list in verse 1 is the law's list. Deuteronomy names the nations of Canaan (Deut 7:1) and, separately, Ammon, Moab and Egypt (23:3-7); several of those peoples had long since ceased to exist. The officials are describing their neighbours in the vocabulary of the Torah, and the Torah had given the reason: they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods (Deut 7:4). The issue was never blood. Ruth was a Moabite, and she is David's great-grandmother — because she said your God my God (Ruth 1:16).
verseByVerse.examples: Faced with the same sin a few years later, Nehemiah beat some of them and pulled out their hair (Neh 13:25). Ezra pulled out his own. Both men were grieved; only one of them sat down in the dust with the guilty and made their sin his own before God.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things had been done, the officials approached me and said, "The people of Israel and the priests and the Levites have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands with their abominations, from the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians, and the Amorites. For they have taken some of their daughters to be wives for themselves and for their sons, so that the holy race has mixed itself with the peoples of the lands. And in this faithlessness the hand of the officials and chief men has been foremost."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After these things had been done, the officials approached me and said, The people of Israel and the priests and the Levites have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands with their abominations.

Ezra has been in Jerusalem for some months, the treasure is weighed, the offerings are made, the king's letters are delivered. And then a group of officials comes to him with what they know is the worst news he could hear.

Listen to the list they give: the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians, and the Amorites. Several of those peoples had not existed as nations for centuries. The Jebusites and the Perizzites were names out of Joshua. This is the law's list — the nations of Canaan named in Deuteronomy 7, with the Ammonites, Moabites and Egyptians of Deuteronomy 23 added. The officials are describing their neighbours in the vocabulary of the Torah. Somebody had been reading the book Ezra brought.

For they have taken some of their daughters to be wives for themselves and for their sons, so that the holy race has mixed itself with the peoples of the lands.

The holy race is, more literally, the holy seed — Isaiah's phrase for the stump left standing when the tree of Israel was cut down: The holy seed is its stump (Isa 6:13). The remnant that had survived the exile was the seed God had kept alive for the future, and now it was being scattered into the fields around it.

It is essential to be clear about what the problem was, or this chapter and the next will be badly misread. It was never race. The law that forbade these marriages gave its reason in the same breath: for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods (Deut 7:4). The concern was a household's worship, not its ancestry. Moabites are on the officials' list — and Ruth was a Moabite, and she is the great-grandmother of David (Ruth 4:17), because she said to Naomi your people shall be my people, and your God my God (Ruth 1:16). And three chapters ago the Passover was eaten by every one who had joined them and separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land (6:21). The door was open to anyone who came to the LORD. What the officials reported was the reverse: Israelites marrying into households that kept their gods.

And the worst line comes last. In this faithlessness the hand of the officials and chief men has been foremost. The leaders had led. The men who should have guarded the community were the ones who had broken the fence first.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as I heard this, I tore my garment and my cloak and pulled hair from my head and beard and sat appalled. Then all who trembled at the words of the God of Israel, because of the faithlessness of the returned exiles, gathered around me while I sat appalled until the evening sacrifice. And at the evening sacrifice I rose from my fasting, with my garment and my cloak torn, and fell upon my knees and spread out my hands to the LORD my God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
As soon as I heard this, I tore my garment and my cloak and pulled hair from my head and beard and sat appalled.

No committee, no inquiry, no statement. He tore his clothes, both layers, and pulled out his own hair and beard, and sat down on the ground unable to move.

Nehemiah dealt with the same sin a few years later, and the contrast is instructive. I confronted them and cursed them and beat some of them and pulled out their hair (Neh 13:25). Nehemiah pulled out other people's hair. Ezra pulled out his own. Both were right to be grieved, and there is a place for Nehemiah's kind of reformer. But Ezra's first instinct was not to punish the guilty. It was to sit down in the dust beside them.

Then all who trembled at the words of the God of Israel, because of the faithlessness of the returned exiles, gathered around me while I sat appalled until the evening sacrifice.

All who trembled at the words of God. Isaiah had said that this is the kind of person God looks at: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word (Isa 66:2). In every congregation there are some of these — people for whom a sentence of Scripture still carries weight — and when a leader sits down in grief over sin, they are the ones who come and sit with him. Nobody organised them. They simply gathered.

Hours passed. He sat there until the evening sacrifice.

And at the evening sacrifice I rose from my fasting, with my garment and my cloak torn, and fell upon my knees and spread out my hands to the LORD my God.

Knees and hands. That is exactly how Solomon prayed at the dedication of the first temple: he knelt on his knees in the presence of all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven (2 Chr 6:13). Solomon knelt to ask God to hear the prayers of a sinning people toward that house. Ezra kneels in the rebuilt house to make one.

And he waited for the evening sacrifice to do it. His prayer was offered at the hour the lamb was on the altar — the confession of guilt joined to the offering for guilt. By the first century, that afternoon offering had become the hour of prayer, the ninth hour (Acts 3:1). It was at the ninth hour that another Man, bearing sins that were not his own, cried out My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Mark 15:34).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–15 — None Can Stand Before You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you, my God, for our iniquities have risen higher than our heads (v. 6). From the fathers to this day the nation has been guilty and handed over (v. 7). But now for a brief moment favor has been shown — a remnant, a secure hold in God's holy place, a little reviving in our slavery (v. 8). For we are slaves. Yet our God has not forsaken us in our slavery (v. 9). And now, O our God, what shall we say after this? For we have forsaken your commandments (vv. 10-12). He has punished them less than they deserved; shall they break his commandments again? (vv. 13-14). O LORD, the God of Israel, you are just ... Behold, we are before you in our guilt, for none can stand before you because of this (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 9 and 10 are the gospel in two sentences. Our God has not forsaken us — we have forsaken your commandments. The whole of 2 Chronicles ran on the rule that if you forsake him, he will forsake you (2 Chr 15:2), and here is a people who had forsaken him again, confessing that he had not forsaken them.
verseByVerse.examples: The prayer ends without asking for anything. No petition for pardon, no proposal, no bargain — only a verdict and a fact: you are just, and none can stand before you. It stops exactly where Psalm 130 pauses: If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? (Ps 130:3). Ezra did not presume the next verse. God supplied it.

verseByVerse.quote: saying: "O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you, my God, for our iniquities have risen higher than our heads, and our guilt has mounted up to the heavens. From the days of our fathers to this day we have been in great guilt. And for our iniquities we, our kings, and our priests have been given into the hand of the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, to plundering, and to utter shame, as it is today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you, my God, for our iniquities have risen higher than our heads, and our guilt has mounted up to the heavens.

Ashamed is the word Ezra used at the river Ahava, when he was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers (8:22). There his shame was before a pagan emperor. Here it is before God, and it is for sins he did not commit.

Watch the pronouns. I am ashamed — and then, in the same breath, our iniquities, our guilt. Ezra had been in the country a few months. He had married nobody. He had every right to say their iniquities, and he never once does. From the first sentence to the last, the guilty party in this prayer is we.

That is what intercession looks like. Not a righteous man reporting other people's failings to God, but a man standing so close to the people he serves that he cannot tell their sin from his own before the throne.

And the picture is a flood. Iniquities risen higher than our heads, guilt mounted up to the heavens. Sin here is not a list of separate offences that could be ticked off one by one; it is water rising over a drowning man.

From the days of our fathers to this day we have been in great guilt. And for our iniquities we, our kings, and our priests have been given into the hand of the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, to plundering, and to utter shame, as it is today.

He sets the present sin inside the whole history. The exile was not bad luck; it was this, the same pattern, and the people standing in Jerusalem are its survivors — as it is today. A man who confesses only the latest sin has not understood the sin.

verseByVerse.quote: But now for a brief moment favor has been shown by the LORD our God, to leave us a remnant and to give us a secure hold within his holy place, that our God may brighten our eyes and grant us a little reviving in our slavery. For we are slaves. Yet our God has not forsaken us in our slavery, but has extended to us his steadfast love before the kings of Persia, to grant us some reviving to set up the house of our God, to repair its ruins, and to give us protection in Judea and Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then, in the middle of the confession, the prayer turns to grace, because the sin cannot be measured until the mercy is measured.

But now for a brief moment favor has been shown by the LORD our God, to leave us a remnant and to give us a secure hold within his holy place, that our God may brighten our eyes and grant us a little reviving in our slavery.

A brief moment. It had been eighty years since Cyrus's decree, and to Ezra it was a moment — a breath of mercy after centuries of judgment.

A secure hold is, in Hebrew, a tent-peg: something driven into the ground that will take a rope and hold. The remnant had not been given a palace in God's holy place. It had been given a peg — a foothold, a place to fasten to. That was enough to hang a life on.

That our God may brighten our eyes. The eyes of a starving man, or a man in the dark, brightening. A little reviving. Not a great restoration; a little life coming back into dead limbs. Every phrase is modest, and every phrase is gratitude.

For we are slaves. They were still subjects of Persia, paying its tribute, living in a province of its empire. The return had not ended their bondage.

Yet our God has not forsaken us in our slavery, but has extended to us his steadfast love before the kings of Persia, to grant us some reviving to set up the house of our God, to repair its ruins, and to give us protection in Judea and Jerusalem.

Our God has not forsaken us. Hold that sentence, because the next verse will say the opposite of the people. And protection is, literally, a wall — the King James Version renders it so. There was no wall around Jerusalem yet; Nehemiah would not build it for another thirteen years. Ezra thanks God for a wall that did not exist in stone, because God had already put one around them.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, O our God, what shall we say after this? For we have forsaken your commandments, which you commanded by your servants the prophets, saying, 'The land that you are entering, to take possession of it, is a land impure with the impurity of the peoples of the lands, with their abominations that have filled it from end to end with their uncleanness. Therefore do not give your daughters to their sons, neither take their daughters for your sons, and never seek their peace or prosperity, that you may be strong and eat the good of the land and leave it for an inheritance to your children forever.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, O our God, what shall we say after this? For we have forsaken your commandments.

What shall we say. He runs out of words. After all the mercy of the last two verses, there is nothing to say except the truth.

And set this beside the verse before it. Our God has not forsaken us (v. 9). We have forsaken your commandments (v. 10). The two sentences stand side by side in the prayer, and between them is the whole story of grace.

A reader who has come through 2 Chronicles knows the rule those two verbs usually follow. The prophet Azariah stated it to Asa: if you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you (2 Chr 15:2). By that rule, a people who forsook God's commandments should have been forsaken. Ezra confesses that they had forsaken him, and that he had not forsaken them. The rule had been broken — from God's side, in mercy.

Then he quotes the commandments they had broken, and what he quotes is not one verse but the law's whole voice gathered up: The land that you are entering, to take possession of it, is a land impure with the impurity of the peoples of the lands — the language of Leviticus, where the land itself is said to have become unclean and vomited out its inhabitants (Lev 18:24-25). Therefore do not give your daughters to their sons, neither take their daughters for your sons — Deuteronomy 7:3. And never seek their peace or prosperity — Deuteronomy 23:6, which was said of the Ammonites and the Moabites, both of whom are on the officials' list.

He attributes all of it to your servants the prophets, and Moses was the first of them. The law and the prophets spoke with one voice about a household's worship, and the people in Jerusalem had heard it and done the opposite.

verseByVerse.quote: And after all that has come upon us for our evil deeds and for our great guilt, seeing that you, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserved and have given us such a remnant as this, shall we break your commandments again and intermarry with the peoples who practice these abominations? Would you not be angry with us until you consumed us, so that there should be no remnant, nor any to escape? O LORD, the God of Israel, you are just, for we are left a remnant that has escaped, as it is today. Behold, we are before you in our guilt, for none can stand before you because of this."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after all that has come upon us for our evil deeds and for our great guilt, seeing that you, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserved and have given us such a remnant as this, shall we break your commandments again?

Less than our iniquities deserved. The exile was terrible — the burned city, the dead, the seventy years — and Ezra says it was less than they deserved. He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities (Ps 103:10). And having been let off so lightly, they had gone straight back to the sin that caused it. Again. That is the word that breaks him.

Would you not be angry with us until you consumed us, so that there should be no remnant, nor any to escape? The question is not rhetorical. He is asking whether God would be within his rights to finish them, and he knows the answer.

O LORD, the God of Israel, you are just, for we are left a remnant that has escaped, as it is today.

You are just. It is the confession Rehoboam and his princes made when Shishak was at the gates — The LORD is righteous (2 Chr 12:6) — the first time in 2 Chronicles that anyone humbled himself. A confession that begins by agreeing with God's verdict is the only kind that has ever been heard.

Behold, we are before you in our guilt, for none can stand before you because of this.

And there the prayer ends. There is no request. He does not ask God to forgive them, or to spare them, or to show them what to do. He lays the guilt down in front of a just God and says that nobody can stand, and stops.

It is the exact place where a psalm pauses: If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? (Ps 130:3). Ezra had reached that sentence, and he did not presume to say the next one. He left it to God.

God has said it. But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared (Ps 130:4). And the reason he can say it without being unjust is the Man who, at the hour of the evening prayer, stood where Ezra's people could not stand, carried iniquities that had risen higher than all our heads, and was forsaken so that we would not be. Now the verb has changed. Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand (Rom 5:2). None could stand. In him, we stand.

9.theology:
Ezra confesses sins he did not commit, in the first person plural, from the first sentence to the last. That is intercession: standing so close to the people that their guilt cannot be told from one's own before God. It is the shadow of the one Intercessor who bore sins that were not his.

Verses 9-10 put the gospel in two sentences — our God has not forsaken us; we have forsaken your commandments. By the rule of 2 Chronicles 15:2 the second should have produced the opposite of the first. Mercy broke the rule from God's side.

And the prayer stops at none can stand before you, exactly where Psalm 130 asks who could stand? It presumes nothing. God answers with the next verse — with you there is forgiveness — and the New Testament finishes the thought: this grace in which we stand (Rom 5:2).
9.examples:
The officials described their neighbours with a list of nations that had not existed for centuries — the list in Deuteronomy.

Ruth was a Moabite, and she is David's great-grandmother, because she said your God my God.

Nehemiah pulled out other people's hair over this sin; Ezra pulled out his own.

Nobody organised the people who trembled at God's word; they came and sat down with him.

Ezra knelt and spread his hands exactly as Solomon had at the dedication of the first temple.

He had married nobody, and he never once said their sin.

He thanked God for a wall thirteen years before Nehemiah built one.

The prayer asks for nothing.

10.overview:
While Ezra prays, a great assembly gathers and weeps, and Shecaniah — from a family on the coming list — speaks for them: We have broken faith ... but even now there is hope for Israel; let us covenant to put away these wives, according to the law; arise ... be strong and do it (vv. 1-4). Ezra puts the people under oath, fasts through the night as Moses did, and a summons calls every exile to Jerusalem within three days (vv. 5-8). In the December rain the assembly trembles, confesses, and agrees — and wisely asks that the cases be heard properly, town by town, over time; four men dissent (vv. 9-15). Named examiners work for three months and finish a year to the day after Ezra left Babylon (vv. 16-17). The list of the 111 men follows, beginning with the high priest's own family and every priestly house that had come home, and the book ends with the children (vv. 18-44).

The issue was worship, not blood — Ruth the Moabite is in David's line, and anyone who left the peoples' uncleanness was welcome (6:21). And for a Christian the New Testament answers the chapter directly: a believer married to an unbeliever should not divorce, for the spouse is made holy and the children ... are holy (1 Cor 7:12-14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Even Now There Is Hope for Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While Ezra prays and weeps before the house of God, a very great assembly of men, women, and children gathers to him, weeping bitterly (v. 1). Shecaniah speaks for them: We have broken faith with our God and have married foreign women from the peoples of the land, but even now there is hope for Israel in spite of this (v. 2). Let us covenant to put away these wives and their children, according to the law (v. 3). Arise, for it is your task, and we are with you; be strong and do it (v. 4). Ezra puts the leaders and all Israel under oath (v. 5), then spends the night in a chamber of the temple neither eating bread nor drinking water (v. 6). A summons goes out: every returned exile to Jerusalem within three days, on pain of forfeiture and exclusion (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 2 puts confession and hope in one breath. Shecaniah does not soften the sin — we have broken faith, the word for treachery in holy things — and he does not despair of it: even now there is hope. Repentance needs both. Confession without hope becomes despair, and hope without confession becomes presumption. And the man who said it came from a family on the list.
verseByVerse.examples: Ezra's night without bread or water is Moses' fast after the golden calf: I neither ate bread nor drank water, because of all the sin that you had committed (Deut 9:18). The leader grieves longest for the sin he did not commit, and does it where nobody is watching.

verseByVerse.quote: While Ezra prayed and made confession, weeping and casting himself down before the house of God, a very great assembly of men, women, and children, gathered to him out of Israel, for the people wept bitterly. And Shecaniah the son of Jehiel, of the sons of Elam, addressed Ezra: "We have broken faith with our God and have married foreign women from the peoples of the land, but even now there is hope for Israel in spite of this. Therefore let us make a covenant with our God to put away all these wives and their children, according to the counsel of my lord and of those who tremble at the commandment of our God, and let it be done according to the Law. Arise, for it is your task, and we are with you; be strong and do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Ezra prayed and made confession, weeping and casting himself down before the house of God, a very great assembly of men, women, and children, gathered to him out of Israel, for the people wept bitterly.

He had called no meeting. He had simply lain on the ground in front of the temple and prayed out loud, and the people came — men, women and children — until there was a great crowd round him, all weeping. A leader's honest grief over sin gives other people permission to feel what they have been suppressing.

Then one of them speaks. And Shecaniah the son of Jehiel, of the sons of Elam, addressed Ezra: We have broken faith with our God and have married foreign women from the peoples of the land, but even now there is hope for Israel in spite of this.

Shecaniah was of the family of Elam, and a Jehiel of the sons of Elam appears in the list of offenders at the end of the chapter (v. 26) — very possibly his own father. If so, the man who stood up and named the sin was standing inside it, and he still said we.

And he said two things in one breath that belong together. We have broken faith — the word for treachery in holy things, the sin of Saul and of the last generation before the exile. And: even now there is hope for Israel. Confession without hope turns into despair. Hope without confession turns into presumption. The first real step toward God always has both in it: this is as bad as it is, and he is still who he is.

Therefore let us make a covenant with our God to put away all these wives and their children, according to the counsel of my lord and of those who tremble at the commandment of our God, and let it be done according to the Law.

This proposal is hard to read, and it must be read carefully and honestly, because a Christian reader may be living inside the very situation it describes.

First, what it was about. Not race. The law forbade these marriages for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods (Deut 7:4), and Ezra's prayer has just described the wives' peoples as the peoples who practice these abominations (9:14). Ruth the Moabite, who said your God my God, became David's great-grandmother; and anyone who left the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to worship the LORD was welcome at the Passover (6:21). The problem was households in which the gods of Canaan were being brought into the remnant God had just rescued from exile for precisely that sin. The prophet Malachi, preaching in the same generation, names the same sin — Judah ... has married the daughter of a foreign god — and condemns in the same breath the men who had divorced the wife of your youth to do it (Mal 2:11, 14).

Second, it belonged to its moment. A tiny community, a few thousand families holding the promise of the Messiah's line in a province of the Persian empire, was being dissolved back into the religion God had exiled it for. Nehemiah reminded them what it had done to Solomon, beloved of God, whom foreign women led into sin (Neh 13:26).

Third, and plainly, it is not what God asks of a Christian today. The apostle answered this question directly for the church: if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him (1 Cor 7:12-13). And he gives the reason, which turns Ezra's situation inside out: For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy (7:14). Under the new covenant the holiness runs from the believer into the home, not the uncleanness from the unbeliever into the believer. A Christian who marries is to marry only in the Lord (7:39); a Christian already married to an unbeliever is to stay, and love, and pray.

Then Shecaniah turns to Ezra. Arise, for it is your task, and we are with you; be strong and do it. The reform was proposed by the people, not imposed on them. They asked their leader to lead them in what they had already decided.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Ezra arose and made the leading priests and Levites and all Israel take an oath that they would do as had been said. So they took the oath. Then Ezra withdrew from before the house of God and went to the chamber of Jehohanan the son of Eliashib, where he spent the night, neither eating bread nor drinking water, for he was mourning over the faithlessness of the exiles. And a proclamation was made throughout Judah and Jerusalem to all the returned exiles that they should assemble at Jerusalem, and that if anyone did not come within three days, by order of the officials and the elders all his property should be forfeited, and he himself banned from the congregation of the exiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Ezra arose and made the leading priests and Levites and all Israel take an oath that they would do as had been said. So they took the oath. An oath binds a community to its better judgment before its worse judgment can recover.

And then Ezra did something that did not need to be recorded. Then Ezra withdrew from before the house of God and went to the chamber of Jehohanan the son of Eliashib, where he spent the night, neither eating bread nor drinking water, for he was mourning over the faithlessness of the exiles.

The oath was taken; the public business was done; he could have gone home satisfied. He went into a side room and fasted through the night instead. And the words are Moses' words after the golden calf: I lay prostrate before the LORD ... forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water, because of all the sin that you had committed (Deut 9:18). The shepherd grieves longest for the sin he did not commit, and does it where nobody is watching.

Then the summons, and it is severe: every returned exile to Jerusalem within three days, and anyone who does not come forfeits his property and is cut off from the congregation. The officials and elders meant it. What was at stake was not a point of etiquette but whether the community would remain the people of God at all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — Trembling Because of This Matter and Because of the Heavy Rain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the twentieth of the ninth month the men of Judah and Benjamin sit in the square before the house of God, trembling because of this matter and because of the heavy rain (v. 9). Ezra stands: You have broken faith and married foreign women ... Now then make confession to the LORD ... and do his will (vv. 10-11). It is so; we must do as you have said — but the people are many, the rain is heavy, and this is not a task for one day or two; let the officials act for the assembly, with the elders and judges of each town, at appointed times (vv. 12-14). Four men oppose it (v. 15). Ezra appoints heads of families by name, and from the first of the tenth month to the first day of the first month they had come to the end of all the men who had married foreign women (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The reform is done by procedure, not by mob. A proposal from the people, an oath, a public assembly, a considered delay, local elders and judges, named examiners, and three months of case after case. Serious sin in a community is not dealt with in an afternoon, and the book shows the patience as well as the resolve.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 15 records dissent and does not explain it. Two men opposed, two supported them, and the narrator gives their names and moves on. We do not know whether they thought the measure too harsh, the delay too long, or something else entirely. The Bible does not pretend that the people of God were unanimous about the most painful decision they made.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the men of Judah and Benjamin assembled at Jerusalem within the three days. It was the ninth month, on the twentieth day of the month. And all the people sat in the open square before the house of God, trembling because of this matter and because of the heavy rain. And Ezra the priest stood up and said to them, "You have broken faith and married foreign women, and so increased the guilt of Israel. Now then make confession to the LORD, the God of your fathers and do his will. Separate yourselves from the peoples of the land and from the foreign wives."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then all the men of Judah and Benjamin assembled at Jerusalem within the three days. It was the ninth month, on the twentieth day of the month. And all the people sat in the open square before the house of God, trembling because of this matter and because of the heavy rain.

The ninth month is December, the beginning of the winter rains in Jerusalem. Picture the square: thousands of men sitting on the wet stones in front of the temple in a downpour, soaked to the skin, shaking.

And the text is gloriously honest about why they were shaking: because of this matter and because of the heavy rain. Part of it was conviction and part of it was cold. Scripture does not pretend that the people of God, even in a solemn hour, stop being bodies.

And Ezra the priest stood up and said to them, You have broken faith and married foreign women, and so increased the guilt of Israel. Now then make confession to the LORD, the God of your fathers and do his will.

In his prayer he had said we. Now, speaking to the people, he says you. Both are right. Before God the leader stands inside the people's sin; before the people he must name it without softening it. And the order is exact: confession first, to the LORD; then obedience. What is done in the square has to begin with what is said to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the assembly answered with a loud voice, "It is so; we must do as you have said. But the people are many, and it is a time of heavy rain; we cannot stand in the open. Nor is this a task for one day or for two, for we have greatly transgressed in this matter. Let our officials stand for the whole assembly. Let all in our cities who have taken foreign wives come at appointed times, and with them the elders and judges of every city, until the fierce wrath of our God over this matter is turned away from us." Only Jonathan the son of Asahel and Jahzeiah the son of Tikvah opposed this, and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite supported them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole assembly answered with a loud voice: It is so; we must do as you have said.

Wet, cold and convicted, they agree. And then, in the same breath, somebody talks sense.

But the people are many, and it is a time of heavy rain; we cannot stand in the open. Nor is this a task for one day or for two, for we have greatly transgressed in this matter. Let our officials stand for the whole assembly. Let all in our cities who have taken foreign wives come at appointed times, and with them the elders and judges of every city.

That is not evasion. It is wisdom. Every case involved a household, a wife, very often children, property, and a town where everyone knew everyone. Cases like that cannot be settled by acclamation in a rainstorm. They need local elders who know the families, and time. The people who proposed the reform also proposed that it be done properly.

Only Jonathan the son of Asahel and Jahzeiah the son of Tikvah opposed this, and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite supported them.

The book records the opposition by name and does not tell us what it was. Perhaps they thought the delay too long; perhaps they thought the whole measure too hard; perhaps something else. The narrator neither condemns nor explains them. It is a small mark of honesty in a book that could easily have presented a unanimous people. A Shabbethai is among the Levites who, years later, helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it (Neh 8:7). If it is the same man, dissent on one hard question did not remove him from the ministry of the word.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the returned exiles did so. Ezra the priest selected men, heads of fathers' houses, according to their fathers' houses, each of them designated by name. On the first day of the tenth month they sat down to examine the matter; and by the first day of the first month they had come to the end of all the men who had married foreign women.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the returned exiles did so. Ezra the priest selected men, heads of fathers' houses, according to their fathers' houses, each of them designated by name. On the first day of the tenth month they sat down to examine the matter; and by the first day of the first month they had come to the end of all the men who had married foreign women.

Named examiners, sitting case by case, for three months. This is how a community of God deals with serious sin: not by panic, not by rumour, not by a crowd, but by known people with a responsibility, taking the time each case requires.

And look at the date they finished: the first day of the first month. Ezra had left Babylon on the first day of the first month, a year before (7:9). A year to the day from the start of the journey, the hardest part of his commission was complete.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–44 — All These Had Married Foreign Women
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The list begins with the priests: some of the sons of Jeshua the son of Jozadak and his brothers, who give their hand to put away their wives and bring a ram of the flock for their guilt (vv. 18-19), then the sons of Immer, Harim and Pashhur (vv. 20-22), six Levites, a singer and three gatekeepers (vv. 23-24), and eighty-four men of Israel, family by family (vv. 25-43). All these had married foreign women, and some of the women had even borne children (v. 44). And there the book ends.
verseByVerse.theology: The four priestly families on this list — Jeshua, Immer, Harim, Pashhur — are the four that came home in chapter 2 (2:36-39). Not one priestly house was untouched, and the high priest's own family heads the list. The guilt offering they bring is the one Leviticus prescribes for a breach of faith in holy things: a ram from the flock (Lev 5:15).
verseByVerse.examples: The book ends with the children, and it does not tell us what became of them. A Christian reading this must hear the New Testament's word for his own home, and it runs the other way: a believer married to an unbeliever should not divorce, for the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife ... Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy (1 Cor 7:12-14).

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were found some of the sons of the priests who had married foreign women: Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah, some of the sons of Jeshua the son of Jozadak and his brothers. They pledged themselves to put away their wives, and their guilt offering was a ram of the flock for their guilt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there were found some of the sons of the priests who had married foreign women: Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah, some of the sons of Jeshua the son of Jozadak and his brothers.

The list begins at the top. Jeshua the son of Jozadak is the high priest who built the altar in chapter 3 and laid the foundation with Zerubbabel. It was his family that Zechariah saw standing before the angel in filthy garments (Zech 3:3). Two generations later, his own descendants are the first names on the list of the guilty. No house in Israel was too close to the altar to be exempt.

They pledged themselves to put away their wives, and their guilt offering was a ram of the flock for their guilt.

Pledged themselves is, literally, gave their hand — the gesture of solemn commitment. And the offering is exact. Leviticus prescribes it for a breach of faith in the holy things of the LORD: a ram without blemish out of the flock (Lev 5:15). The word for the breach is the very word Shecaniah and Ezra used — we have broken faith (vv. 2, 10). The altar built before the temple in chapter 3 was doing what it was built for. There was a sacrifice even for this.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the sons of Immer: Hanani and Zebadiah. Of the sons of Harim: Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel, and Uzziah. Of the sons of Pashhur: Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethanel, Jozabad, and Elasah. Of the Levites: Jozabad, Shimei, Kelaiah (that is, Kelita), Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer. Of the singers: Eliashib. Of the gatekeepers: Shallum, Telem, and Uri.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the other priestly houses: two of the sons of Immer, five of the sons of Harim, six of the sons of Pashhur. Seventeen priests in all.

Turn back to chapter 2. The priests who came home with Zerubbabel were four families: Jedaiah of the house of Jeshua, Immer, Pashhur and Harim (2:36-39). Those are exactly the four on this list. Every priestly family that returned from exile was implicated.

Then six Levites, one singer, three gatekeepers. The Levites Ezra had to send for at the canal (8:15-20) were not immune either.

Two of those Levite names should be held onto. Kelaiah (that is, Kelita) — the narrator stops to tell us the other name he was known by — and Jozabad. When Ezra later read the law to the whole city, the Levites who went among the people and helped the people to understand the Law included a Jozabad and a Kelita (Neh 8:7). If they are the same men — and the narrator's aside suggests a Kelita his readers would recognise — then two Levites who put away their wives in this December became, a dozen years on, teachers of the book that had convicted them. Forgiven men make the most careful teachers.
