verseByVerse.commentary:
And of Israel — the laymen, family by family. Seven of the sons of Parosh, six of Elam, six of Zattu, four of Bebai, six of Bani, eight of Pahath-moab, eight of Harim, seven of Hashum, twelve more of Bani, thirteen of Binnui, seven of Nebo. Eighty-four men under eleven family names.

Almost every one of those family names is on the list of chapter 2, the families who walked home with Zerubbabel, and several are on Ezra's own list in chapter 8. These were not outsiders. They were the grandsons of the people who wept and shouted over the foundation.

Add the whole list and it comes to a hundred and eleven men. Out of a community of tens of thousands, it is a small number. It is not a small matter, because a hundred and eleven households at the top of a small people — priests, Levites and the heads of the leading families — set the direction for everyone else.

And the Bible keeps every name. Not to shame them; they had confessed and brought their offering. It keeps them the way it kept the names of chapter 2 — because God deals with people, not categories, and a list of the forgiven is still a list of his.

verseByVerse.quote: All these had married foreign women, and some of the women had even borne children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All these had married foreign women, and some of the women had even borne children.

And there the book ends. No feast, no dedication, no summary. A list, and a line about the children.

It is an uncomfortable ending, and it is meant to be. The narrator does not hide the cost. There were women and children in these homes, and the book does not tell us where they went or how they lived. Reform in that hour was real, and it was painful, and Scripture records the pain without pretending it away.

Which is why a Christian must read the last verse of Ezra with the New Testament open. The apostle's word to a believer married to an unbeliever is the opposite of this chapter's covenant: he should not divorce her — because as it is, they are holy (1 Cor 7:12-14). The children of such a home are not to be sent away. They are within the reach of the covenant through the believing parent. What changed between Ezra and Paul was not that God grew less holy. It was that the Holy One himself had come, and holiness now spreads outward from those who belong to him.

And the book that ends with foreign wives sent away is followed, in the fullness of time, by a gospel that brings the foreigners in. Remember that you were at that time ... alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise ... But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ ... So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Eph 2:12-13, 19).

Not by lowering the standard of this chapter — the standard was never lower — but by a Bridegroom who took a bride from among the nations, unclean and far off, and instead of putting her away, gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle (Eph 5:25-27). Ezra's community could keep itself holy only by sending the foreigner away. Christ makes the foreigner holy and keeps her.

10.theology:
Shecaniah's even now there is hope (v. 2) holds together what repentance needs: an honest name for the sin and a settled confidence in God's mercy. And the guilt offering of v. 19 is Leviticus 5:15's ram for a breach of faith — the altar of chapter 3 doing what it was built for.

The chapter belongs to a unique moment, when a tiny remnant carrying the promise of the Messiah's line was being drawn back into the idolatry it had been exiled for; Malachi condemns the same sin in the same generation (Mal 2:11). The new covenant reverses the direction of the danger: holiness now flows from the believer into the marriage (1 Cor 7:14). The book that ends with foreigners sent away gives way to a gospel in which Christ brings them near (Eph 2:13) and makes his bride holy rather than putting her away (Eph 5:25-27).
10.examples:
The man who first named the sin came from a family on the list, and he still said we, and even now there is hope.

After the public oath, Ezra went into a side room and fasted all night, as Moses did after the golden calf.

They sat in the square in December, trembling because of the sin and because of the rain.

The people who proposed the reform also proposed that it be done properly, case by case, with local elders.

Four dissenters are named, and the book never says what they objected to.

Every priestly family that came home in chapter 2 is on the list, and the high priest's family is first.

Two Levites on the list may be the same men who later helped the whole city understand the law.

A Christian married to an unbeliever is told by the apostle to stay: as it is, they are holy.
